about: Fuori model syllabus for Italian, A1–C1 (docs/teach-plan.md → Magda). Built 2026-10-22 from every course book read in full (Nuovissimo Progetto italiano 1a, 1B, 2, 3; Proudfoot; English Grammar for Students of Italian; Beginner's Guide; Le preposizioni italiane; Must-Know Italian Slang), lined up and reordered for a newcomer living in Italy, then reviewed by a second teacher. About the language and real-life situations only, not the game's places or mechanics. Readable version: docs/syllabus-it.md. Word list: content/it/syllabus-words.csv.

units.title: Greet and take leave
units.can_do: Greet people and say goodbye at any time of day, with tu or Lei as the moment calls for.
situations: entering and leaving a shop or bar
meeting a neighbour on the stairs
greeting an older person or an official
stopping a stranger in the street

frames.it: Buongiorno!
frames.en: Good morning!
frames.note: Until lunch or early afternoon. Also works as 'hello' and 'goodbye' in shops.

frames.it: Buonasera, signora.
frames.en: Good evening, madam.
frames.note: From mid-afternoon, roughly when shops reopen after lunch.

frames.it: Salve!
frames.en: Hello!
frames.note: Neutral and safe with anyone when you're unsure whether to use tu or Lei.

frames.it: Ciao! Come stai?
frames.en: Hi! How are you?
frames.note: tu: friends, children, and people who use tu with you. Ciao also means 'bye'.

frames.it: Buongiorno, come sta?
frames.en: Good morning, how are you?
frames.note: Lei: strangers, shopkeepers, older people.

frames.it: Bene, grazie. E Lei? / E tu?
frames.en: Fine, thanks. And you?

frames.it: Senta, scusi...
frames.en: Excuse me...
frames.note: To get a stranger's attention. With a friend: Senti, scusa...

frames.it: Arrivederci, buona giornata!
frames.en: Goodbye, have a good day!
frames.note: In the evening: Buona serata!

frames.it: Grazie, anche a Lei! / Altrettanto!
frames.en: Thanks, you too! / Same to you!
frames.note: With tu: Anche a te!

frames.it: A domani! / Ci vediamo!
frames.en: See you tomorrow! / See you!

grammar.point: tu and Lei as two sets of chunks
grammar.explain: Italian has a friendly 'you' (tu) and a polite 'you' (Lei), and Lei takes the same verb form as 'he' or 'she'.

examples.en: How are you? (tu / Lei)
Excuse me! (tu / Lei)
And you? (tu / Lei)

grammar.trap: Using tu with a shopkeeper or an older stranger sounds overfamiliar. When in doubt, use Lei until they offer tu.

grammar.explain: To say how you are, Italian uses stare, not essere.

examples.en: I'm well, thanks.
How are you, madam?

grammar.trap: English 'I am fine' tempts you to say 'sono bene', which is wrong. Say 'sto bene'.

grammar.explain: Buongiorno covers the morning and early afternoon, buonasera the rest of the day, and buonanotte is only for bedtime.

examples.en: Good morning! (10 a.m.)
Good evening! (5 p.m.)
Good night, see you tomorrow!

grammar.trap: Buonanotte is not 'good evening': saying it when you walk into a bar at 9 p.m. sounds like you're going to bed. Buonasera starts much earlier than English 'good evening'.

vocabulary.en: doctor; title for any graduate (dottoressa for a woman)
day (as it is lived: buona giornata)

pronunciation: Double consonants are held longer, and the vowel before them is short: arrivederci, mattina, dottore, dottoressa. A single consonant is quick: sera, domani.
gn sounds like the ny in 'canyon': signora, signore. It is one sound, not g + n.

common_errors.why: How you are uses stare, not essere.

common_errors.wrong: Buonanotte! (walking into a bar at 9 p.m.)
common_errors.why: Buonanotte is only said when someone is going to bed.

common_errors.wrong: Ciao, signora! (to a shopkeeper you've just met)
common_errors.why: Ciao belongs to tu; strangers and shopkeepers get Lei greetings.
With Lei the verb is the 'he/she' form.

units.culture: Italians greet when they walk into a shop, a bar, a lift or a waiting room, and say goodbye when they leave; walking in or out in silence comes across as rude. Buonasera starts surprisingly early, around 3 or 4 p.m.
units.evidence: Without being prompted, the learner greets on arrival with the right word for the time of day, uses Lei with an older or unfamiliar character and tu with a friend, answers 'come sta?' with 'bene, grazie, e Lei?', and leaves with a goodbye in the matching register.
sources: P1a Intro, U1 E (greetings box, formal street dialogue)
Proudfoot U1 (tu/Lei, greetings by time of day, titles)
EGSI ch.13 (familiar and formal you), ch.20 (stare for health)
BG ch.2 (tu/Lei table)

units.title: When you don't understand
units.can_do: Say you didn't understand, ask someone to repeat or slow down, and ask what a word means or how to say something.
functions: say how much Italian you speak
situations: any conversation that goes too fast
a counter where you missed the price
meeting a word you don't know

frames.it: Scusi, non ho capito.
frames.en: Sorry, I didn't understand.

frames.it: Può ripetere, per favore?
frames.en: Could you repeat that, please?
frames.note: With tu: Puoi ripetere?

frames.it: Più piano, per favore.
frames.en: More slowly, please.

frames.it: Cosa vuol dire “scontrino”?
frames.en: What does “scontrino” mean?

frames.it: Come si dice “receipt” in italiano?
frames.en: How do you say “receipt” in Italian?

frames.it: Come si scrive?
frames.en: How do you spell it?

frames.it: Può dirlo in inglese?
frames.en: Could you say it in English?
frames.note: A fixed chunk; the lo ('it') stuck to the verb is taught at A2.

frames.it: Parlo solo un po' d'italiano.
frames.en: I only speak a little Italian.

frames.it: Ah, ho capito, grazie!
frames.en: Ah, got it, thanks!

frames.it: Ha capito?
frames.en: Did you understand?
frames.note: With tu: Hai capito?

grammar.point: non goes right before the verb
grammar.explain: To make a sentence negative, put non immediately before the verb, with no helper word like 'do'.

examples.en: I didn't understand.
I don't speak Italian well.

grammar.trap: There is no Italian 'do' or 'did': don't look for a word for it. Just put non before the verb.

grammar.point: può + infinitive as a polite request
grammar.explain: Può ('can you', Lei) followed by a verb in its basic form makes a polite request.

examples.en: Could you repeat that?
Could you speak more slowly?
Could you repeat that? (tu)

grammar.trap: No 'to' between the two verbs: 'può ripetere', not 'può a ripetere'.

grammar.point: ho capito / non ho capito as fixed forms
grammar.explain: Italians say 'I understood / I didn't understand' about what was just said, and you can use these before learning the past tense.

examples.en: I didn't catch that.
Got it! / I see!

grammar.trap: 'Non capisco' means you can't follow in general; for something just said, Italians use the past: 'non ho capito'.

grammar.point: come si dice? / come si scrive? as fixed chunks
grammar.explain: Si + verb means 'one' or 'you' in general, so 'come si dice?' is 'how does one say?'.

examples.en: How do you say “receipt”?
What does “piano” mean?

grammar.trap: English 'what does it mean' has a 'does' that disappears: 'Cosa vuol dire?', with no extra verb.

vocabulary.en: foreign; a foreigner (straniera for a woman)

pronunciation: Stress: capìto (ca-PI-to), ripètere (ri-PE-te-re), parlo (PAR-lo). Più ends on a stressed ù: pi-Ù.
Learn the letter names for spelling: a, bi, ci, di, e, effe, gi, acca, i, elle, emme, enne, o, pi, cu, erre, esse, ti, u, vu, zeta.

common_errors.why: The past needs ho in front of capito.
Parola is feminine, so 'this' is questa.
No subject pronoun: può is already 'you (Lei)', puoi is 'you (tu)'.
With si the verb is the 'he/she' form.

units.culture: To say 'Sorry? / Pardon?' Italians say 'Come?' or 'Scusi?'; a bare 'Cosa?' can sound blunt. Most people are pleased you're trying, but many speed up or switch to English, so a friendly 'più piano, per favore' is normal and expected.
recycles: a1-01: tu and Lei pairs (può / puoi)
units.evidence: When a character goes too fast or uses an unknown word, the learner repairs in Italian (non ho capito, può ripetere?, più piano, cosa vuol dire...?, come si dice...?) instead of going silent or switching to English, then confirms with 'ho capito'.
sources: P1a U2 (Professore, può ripetere, per favore?; polite requests with modals)
P1a §5, P1B §5, P2 §5, Proudfoot §5 (no book teaches a repair set: gap)
EGSI ch.15 (non), ch.16 (questions), ch.31 (si in come si dice?)
BG ch.1 (alphabet and sounds)

units.title: Introduce yourself as a newcomer
units.can_do: Say who you are, where you're from, where you live, why you're here and for how long, and ask the same back.
functions: say you live here, not on holiday
answer a welcome or a compliment
situations: first chat with someone who asks where you're from
the first day of a language course

frames.it: Mi chiamo … E Lei, come si chiama?
frames.en: My name's … And what's your name?
frames.note: With tu: E tu, come ti chiami?

frames.it: Piacere!

frames.it: Sono americano, di …
frames.en: I'm American, from …
frames.note: A woman says americana. Di + your city.

frames.it: Di dove sei? / Di dov'è?

frames.it: Sono qui per imparare l'italiano.
frames.en: I'm here to learn Italian.

frames.it: Sono in pensione. / Lavoro come …
frames.en: I'm retired. / I work as a …

frames.it: Ben arrivato! / Ben arrivata!
frames.en: Welcome!
frames.note: Said to a man / to a woman.

grammar.point: essere in the present: sono, sei, è
grammar.explain: Essere is 'to be', and the subject pronoun is usually left out because the verb already shows who.

examples.en: I'm American.
Are you from Rome? (tu)
Are you here on holiday? (Lei)

grammar.trap: Saying 'io sono' every time sounds emphatic, as if contrasting yourself with someone else. Just say 'sono'.

grammar.point: chiamarsi as a chunk: mi chiamo, ti chiami, si chiama
grammar.explain: Italians say 'I call myself' to give their name.

examples.en: My name's Anna.
What's your name? (Lei)

grammar.trap: The question uses come ('how'), not cosa: 'Come ti chiami?', never 'Cosa ti chiami?'.

grammar.point: -are verbs for io, tu and Lei
grammar.explain: Regular -are verbs end in -o for 'I', -i for 'you (tu)' and -a for 'you (Lei)' and 'he/she'.

examples.en: I live in the centre.
Where do you live? (tu)
Where do you live? (Lei)

grammar.trap: With Lei use the -a ending, the 'he/she' form: 'Dove abita?', not 'Dove abiti?'.

grammar.explain: Nationality words ending in -o change to -a for a woman; those ending in -e stay the same.

examples.en: I'm American. (man / woman)
I'm English. (man or woman)

grammar.trap: Nationalities are written with a small letter in Italian: americano, inglese.

grammar.point: di, a and in with places
grammar.explain: Use di + city for where you're from, a + city and in + country for where you live.

examples.en: I'm from Chicago.
I live in Florence.
I live in Italy.

grammar.trap: 'I'm from' is 'sono di', not 'sono da'; and 'in Florence' is 'a Firenze', not 'in Firenze'.

grammar.explain: For something that started in the past and is still going on, Italian uses the present tense with da.

examples.it: Sono in Italia da tre settimane.
examples.en: I've been in Italy for three weeks.
I've been studying Italian for a month.

grammar.trap: Don't copy the English past: 'Sono stato qui per tre settimane' means the stay is over.

pronunciation: Hold double consonants: anno (year) has a long n; ano with a short n means 'anus'. Also settimana, abbastanza.
ch before i or e sounds like k: chiamo is 'KYAH-mo'. Without the h, ci and ce sound like English ch: città, piacere.

common_errors.why: Origin with essere takes di.
Cities take a; countries and regions take in.

common_errors.wrong: Sono qui per tre settimane. (meaning you arrived three weeks ago)
common_errors.why: Da + present is for something still going on; per sounds like a planned length of stay.
Mi chiamo already contains the verb.
The adjective agrees with the speaker.

units.culture: 'Di dove sei?' is one of the first things Italians ask, because where you come from matters a lot here. Saying you live here, not that you're on holiday, changes the conversation: people start treating you as a neighbour, and they'll often compliment your Italian (just say 'Grazie, ma sto imparando!').
recycles: a1-02: Parlo solo un po' d'italiano
units.evidence: Asked where they're from, the learner answers with di + city, says they live here (abito a/in ...) and how long they've been here with da + present, asks the same back in the right register, and the adjectives agree with their own gender.
sources: P1a Intro C, E (essere, chiamarsi, nationalities)
P1a U1 C (bus-stop meeting: di dove sei? sei qui per lavoro? da quanto tempo?), U1 E (formal: ed è qui in vacanza?)
P1a workbook U1 ex.16 (Alicia's self-introduction)
Proudfoot U1 (personal information, di + city), U11 (da + present)
PREP (di / da / a / in)
EGSI ch.12, ch.14

grammar.point: Noun gender and the indefinite article
grammar.explain: 'A/an' is un for most masculine nouns, uno before s + consonant or z, una for feminine nouns and un' before a feminine noun starting with a vowel.

examples.en: a coffee, a croissant
a spritz, a yogurt
a fresh juice, an orangeade

grammar.trap: Learn each noun with its article, because the ending doesn't always show the gender. Un' with an apostrophe is only for feminine words.

grammar.explain: Most nouns change their last vowel in the plural (-o to -i, -a to -e), but words ending in an accented vowel or a consonant don't change.

examples.en: two cappuccinos, two croissants
two fresh juices

examples.it: due caffè, due tè, due spritz
examples.en: two coffees, two teas, two spritzes

grammar.trap: Never add an English -s: 'due caffè', not 'due caffès'.

grammar.point: vorrei as a fixed polite phrase
grammar.explain: Vorrei means 'I would like' and is the polite way to ask for anything; you can use it now and learn its grammar at A2.

examples.en: I'd like a coffee.
I'd like a glass of water.

grammar.trap: 'Voglio' ('I want') sounds pushy at a counter. Use vorrei, per me, or just the item + per favore.

grammar.explain: Italians 'take' food and drink, so prendere is the verb for 'have' when ordering.

examples.en: I'll have a croissant.
What are you having? (tu)
What are you having? (Lei)

grammar.trap: Don't use avere for ordering: 'ho un caffè' means 'I've got a coffee', not 'I'll have one'.

vocabulary.en: with a dash of milk (caffè macchiato)
bar person (la barista for a woman)
to offer; to pay for someone

pronunciation: Double consonants are long: cappuccino has a long pp and a long cc; cornetto a long tt. Caffè is stressed on the last syllable: caf-FÈ.
c before i or e sounds like 'ch' (cappuccino: cap-poo-CHEE-no); before a, o, u it is 'k' (caffè, cornetto).

common_errors.why: Masculine words starting with s + consonant take uno.
Words ending in an accented vowel don't change in the plural.

common_errors.right: Vorrei un caffè. / Un caffè, per favore.
common_errors.why: Voglio sounds like a demand; vorrei is the polite form.

common_errors.wrong: Un latte, per favore. (wanting a milky coffee)
common_errors.why: Latte on its own is just a glass of milk.

units.culture: In many bars you pay first at the cassa, then hand the scontrino to the barista and order at the counter. Standing at the banco is cheaper than sitting at a table, where there may be table service at a higher price. Cappuccino is a morning drink; after lunch Italians order an espresso.
recycles: a1-03: tu and Lei verb forms (prendi / prende)
units.evidence: The learner orders at least two items with the right articles (un/uno/una/un'), uses vorrei or per me rather than voglio, asks a companion 'cosa prendi?', answers 'al banco' or 'al tavolo', and pluralises correctly when ordering for two.
sources: P1a U4 D (three friends ordering, the listino; ordering box: Cosa prendi? Per me... Vorrei...)
P1a U4 culture: Il bar italiano, Un caffè! (pay first at the cassa, no cappuccino after lunch)
P1a Intro (nouns, plurals), U1 (indefinite article)
P2 U0 (fare lo scontrino)
Proudfoot U2 (identifying things; bar vocabulary; plurals of caffè, bar), U14 (vorrei vs voglio)
EGSI ch.2–4

units.title: Prices, numbers and paying
units.can_do: Ask and understand prices, count well past a hundred, and pay by card or cash.

grammar.explain: Numbers are built as in English (venti + tre = ventitré), but the tens drop their last vowel before uno and otto.

examples.en: 23, 33 (with an accent)

grammar.trap: Mille becomes -mila in the plural (duemila, not duemille), and numbers are written as one word.

grammar.explain: Euro is the same in the singular and plural; cents are centesimi, often left unsaid.

examples.en: one euro, two euros
three euros twenty

grammar.trap: Never 'euros'. And spoken 'quattro e cinquanta' means €4.50; if a price sounds odd, ask again.

grammar.point: costa with one thing, costano with several
grammar.explain: The verb agrees with the thing being priced, which comes after it.

examples.en: How much is the bread?
How much are the biscuits?

grammar.trap: English 'how much is it' has no subject in Italian: just 'quanto costa?'.

grammar.explain: Posso ('can I') followed by a basic verb form asks for permission.

examples.en: Can I pay by card?
Can I pay cash?

grammar.trap: No 'to' and no conjugated second verb: 'posso pagare', not 'posso pago'.

pronunciation: Hold the double t in sette (7) and otto (8), and in diciassette, diciotto. Sei (6) and sette (7) are easy to confuse at speed: listen for the long tt.
Numbers ending in -tré are stressed on the last syllable: ventitré (ven-ti-TRÈ). Plain tre has no accent.

common_errors.why: Euro never changes in the plural.
Several things take the plural costano.
After posso the verb stays in the infinitive.
The tens drop their final vowel before uno and otto.

units.culture: Shops are required to accept cards, but small shops and market stalls still prefer cash for small amounts, so keep some coins: cashiers often ask 'Ha moneta?' to avoid breaking a big note. Take the scontrino when it's handed to you.
recycles: a1-02: Può ripetere? / Più piano (for prices said fast)
a1-04: Un caffè e un cornetto
units.evidence: The learner asks 'quanto costa / quanto costano' with the right number, understands a spoken price well enough to pay or check it back, asks to pay by card, and handles 'Ha moneta?' without switching to English.
sources: P1a Intro (numbers 1–30), U2 (30–2,000), U3 (to a million, prices: Quanto costa questo divano?)
P1B U9 (payment)
Proudfoot U5 (numbers, euro invariable, the quattro cinquanta ambiguity, quanto costa/costano), U8 (posso + infinitive)
BG ch.6 (numbers to 100)

grammar.explain: C'è means 'there is' and ci sono 'there are'; to ask a shop if it has something, say avete ('do you have', plural you).

examples.en: Is there a pharmacy near here?

examples.it: Ci sono due bar in piazza.
examples.en: There are two bars in the square.
Do you have breadsticks?

grammar.trap: Choose by what follows: one thing takes c'è, several take ci sono ('ci sono due bar', not 'c'è due bar').

grammar.point: The definite article: il, lo, l', la, i, gli, le
grammar.explain: 'The' changes with gender, number and the first sound of the next word, following the same pattern as un/uno/una.

examples.en: the bread, the breadsticks
the receipt, the coins
the focaccia, the pastries, the water

grammar.trap: Lo and gli go before s + consonant and z (lo scontrino, gli zii); l' goes before any vowel, but le is never shortened.

grammar.explain: Questo ('this one') and quello ('that one') replace the noun, so you can point when you don't know the word.

examples.en: I'll take this one.
That one there, thanks.
Those there, the pastries.

grammar.trap: There's no word for 'one': say 'questo', never 'questo uno'. If you don't know the gender, masculine questo / questi is fine.

grammar.point: un po' di and del / della for 'some'
grammar.explain: Un po' di ('a bit of') works with anything; del / della are 'some' as fixed chunks for now.

examples.it: Un po' di focaccia, per favore.
examples.en: A bit of focaccia, please.
I'd like some bread.

grammar.trap: Un po' di never changes; del, della and the rest are taught as a system at A2.

grammar.point: mi dà...? as a fixed polite request
grammar.explain: Mi dà...? ('will you give me...?', Lei) is how Italians ask for something across a counter.

examples.it: Mi dà un pane, per favore?
examples.en: Could I have a loaf, please?
Could I have two of these?

grammar.trap: To a shopkeeper it's mi dà (Lei); 'mi dai' is for a friend.

vocabulary.en: pizza by the slice, sold by weight

pronunciation: C'è sounds like 'cheh', but che sounds like 'keh': c'è un bagno? / che cos'è? Hold the double cc in focaccia and the double zz in pizza.
gli sounds like the 'lli' in 'million': gli spiccioli, gli zii. It's one soft sound, not g + l.

common_errors.why: Several things take ci sono.
Lo before s + consonant; l' before a vowel.
Italian has no word for 'one' after questo or quello.

common_errors.wrong: Mi dai un pane? (to a shopkeeper)
common_errors.why: Shopkeepers get the Lei form.

units.culture: In bakeries and pastry shops you don't serve yourself: you ask and point, and the assistant picks. Where there's a ticket dispenser, take a number and wait to be called. Pizza al taglio and bread are often sold by weight, so the assistant cuts a piece and asks 'Così va bene?'.
units.evidence: The learner asks whether a shop has something (avete...?) or whether there is something nearby (c'è...?), uses ci sono for plurals, points with questo / quello lì when the word is missing, and asks with mi dà...? or un po' di....
sources: Proudfoot U2 (Che cos'è? questo; point when you don't know the noun), U3 (c'è / ci sono, ce n'è, un po' di, partitive), U4 (definite article), U5 (questo / quello)
P1a Intro D (definite article), U3 (c'è / ci sono, partitive dei panini)
EGSI ch.4 (articles), ch.5 (partitive), ch.20 (c'è / ecco), ch.44 (questo, quello)

units.title: Where is it? Asking the way
units.can_do: Ask where a place is and follow short directions, helped by gestures and landmarks.
situations: looking for the station, a church or a museum

frames.it: Scusi, dov'è la stazione?
frames.en: Excuse me, where's the station?

frames.it: Scusi, per andare al Duomo?
frames.en: Excuse me, how do I get to the cathedral?

frames.it: È lontano?
frames.en: Is it far?

frames.it: È qui vicino, a due passi.
frames.en: It's close by, just round the corner.

frames.it: Sempre dritto, poi a destra.
frames.en: Straight on, then right.

frames.it: Giri a sinistra al semaforo.
frames.en: Turn left at the traffic lights.

frames.it: È in fondo alla strada, accanto alla chiesa.
frames.en: It's at the end of the street, next to the church.

frames.it: Dritto e poi a sinistra?
frames.en: Straight on and then left?
frames.note: Repeat the directions back to check.

frames.it: Grazie mille, molto gentile!
frames.en: Thanks a lot, very kind!

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Scusi, per andare al Duomo?
lines.en: Excuse me, how do I get to the cathedral?

lines.speaker: shopkeeper
lines.it: Allora... vada dritto fino alla piazza, poi prenda la seconda a destra.
lines.en: Right... go straight on as far as the square, then take the second on the right.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Scusi, non ho capito. Può ripetere più piano?
lines.en: Sorry, I didn't understand. Could you repeat that more slowly?

lines.en: Straight on to the square... then the second street on the right.

lines.en: Got it! Is it far?

lines.speaker: shopkeeper
lines.it: No, no, è a due passi.
lines.en: No, no, it's just round the corner.

grammar.explain: Dov'è asks where one thing is and dove sono where several things are.

examples.en: Where's the stop?
Where are the toilets?

grammar.trap: Dove + è shortens to dov'è in speech and writing; dove sono stays as it is.

grammar.point: Places with a, in and da as chunks
grammar.explain: Some places take a, some in and people's places take da, and you learn each as a set phrase.

examples.it: al bar, alla stazione, al Duomo
examples.en: to/at the bar, the station, the cathedral

examples.it: in piazza, in centro, in farmacia
examples.en: in/to the square, the centre, the pharmacy
at/to the doctor's

grammar.trap: English 'to' and 'at' don't map onto one Italian word; learn the place with its preposition.

grammar.point: a + the article: al, alla, all'
grammar.explain: When a meets il, la or l' they join into one word, and you can use these chunks before learning the whole table at A2.

examples.en: at the traffic lights
to the church
at the corner

grammar.trap: Say 'alla stazione', never 'a la stazione'.

grammar.point: Place words with a: vicino a, accanto a, davanti a, di fronte a, in fondo a
grammar.explain: These place expressions are followed by a, which joins the article.

examples.en: next to the church
in front of the bar
at the end of the street

grammar.trap: Don't drop the a: 'vicino alla chiesa', not 'vicino la chiesa'. A destra and a sinistra never take an article.

grammar.explain: Directions to a stranger come as polite commands whose endings look 'reversed': -are verbs end in -i, others in -a.

examples.en: Turn right.
Go straight on.
Take the first on the left.

grammar.trap: You only need to recognise these now; you'll produce them at B1. Friends use the tu form: gira, vai, prendi.

vocabulary.en: cathedral (the main church of a city)
at the end of, at the bottom of
side, part (da questa parte = this way)

pronunciation: Stress the right syllable: semàforo (se-MA-fo-ro), stazióne (sta-TSIO-ne), sinìstra (si-NI-stra).
Hold the double tt in dritto and the double cc in accanto: short consonants sound foreign.

common_errors.why: A and la always join.
In standard Italian vicino is followed by a.
In piedi means 'standing'; on foot is a piedi.
A destra and a sinistra take no article.

units.culture: Italians give directions with landmarks (the church, the tobacconist, the traffic lights) and plenty of gestures, so watch the hands as well as the words. 'A due passi' can mean anything from one minute to fifteen, and in old town centres street names change every few blocks.
recycles: a1-02: Non ho capito / Può ripetere più piano?
a1-06: C'è una farmacia qui vicino?
units.evidence: The learner asks for a place with dov'è or per andare a...?, checks the directions back with a short summary (dritto e poi a destra?), asks if it's far, and shows they followed the key words (destra, sinistra, dritto, semaforo, in fondo).
sources: P1a U1 C (Scusa, per andare in centro?), U1 E (Scusi, sa dov'è via Alberti?), U3 C (locatives: accanto a, davanti a, vicino a)
Proudfoot U4 (location, dov'è / dove sono, place prepositions), U9 (directions dialogue: vada diritto, giri a sinistra)
PREP (a vs in, fixed place chunks, a piedi)
P1B U10 F (full directions, A2)

units.title: Times, days and opening hours
units.can_do: Ask and tell the time, ask when somewhere opens and closes, and fix a time.
situations: finding a shop closed at lunchtime
a pharmacy's hours and the night rota

frames.it: Scusi, che ore sono?
frames.en: Excuse me, what time is it?
frames.note: Also: Che ora è?

frames.it: Sono le tre e mezza. / È l'una.
frames.en: It's half past three. / It's one o'clock.

frames.it: A che ora apre la farmacia?
frames.en: What time does the pharmacy open?

frames.it: A che ora chiude?
frames.en: What time does it close?

frames.it: Siete aperti la domenica?
frames.en: Are you open on Sundays?

frames.it: Dalle nove all'una e dalle quattro alle otto.
frames.en: From nine to one and from four to eight.

frames.it: Il lunedì mattina siamo chiusi.
frames.en: We're closed on Monday mornings.

frames.it: Torno tra dieci minuti.
frames.en: I'll be back in ten minutes.

frames.it: Ci vediamo alle sei?
frames.en: Shall we meet at six?

lines.speaker: shop assistant

lines.en: We're open from nine to one and from four to eight.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Perfetto, torno stasera. Grazie!
lines.en: Perfect, I'll come back this evening. Thanks!

model_exchanges.situation: Asking the time in the street

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Scusi, che ore sono?
lines.en: Excuse me, what time is it?

lines.speaker: passer-by
lines.it: Sono le due meno un quarto.
lines.en: It's a quarter to two.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Ah, è tardi! Grazie mille.
lines.en: Oh, it's late! Thanks a lot.

lines.speaker: passer-by
lines.it: Prego!
lines.en: You're welcome!

model_exchanges.situation: Fixing a time with a friend (tu)

lines.speaker: friend
lines.it: Ci vediamo stasera?
lines.en: Shall we meet this evening?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Sì! A che ora?
lines.en: Yes! What time?

lines.speaker: friend
lines.it: Alle sei e mezza va bene?
lines.en: Is half past six OK?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Va bene! A stasera!
lines.en: OK! See you tonight!

grammar.point: sono le + hour, but è l'una, è mezzogiorno, è mezzanotte
grammar.explain: Times are plural ('they are the three'), except one o'clock, midday and midnight, which are singular.

examples.en: It's three o'clock.

examples.it: Sono le sette e un quarto.
examples.en: It's a quarter past seven.
It's half past one.

grammar.trap: Never 'è le tre'. And minutes before the hour use meno: 'le otto meno dieci' = ten to eight.

grammar.explain: 'At' a time is alle (all'una), and opening hours are 'from the ... to the ...'.

examples.en: It opens at nine.
It closes at one.
From four to eight.

grammar.trap: Midday and midnight take plain a: 'a mezzogiorno', 'a mezzanotte'.

grammar.explain: Tra (or fra) + an amount of time means 'from now'.

examples.en: I'll be back in ten minutes.
The train leaves in an hour.

grammar.trap: 'In dieci minuti' means 'taking ten minutes' (I can do it in ten minutes), not 'ten minutes from now'.

grammar.explain: Lunedì alone means 'this Monday'; il lunedì means 'on Mondays', every week.

examples.en: On Monday I'm going to the bank.
We're closed on Mondays.

grammar.trap: No word for 'on': not 'in lunedì' or 'a lunedì'.

grammar.explain: Italians use the present tense for things they'll do soon.

examples.en: I'll come back tomorrow.
We'll meet at six.

grammar.trap: You don't need a future tense for plans: 'torno stasera' is natural.

vocabulary.en: half (e mezza / e mezzo = half past)
quarter (e un quarto, meno un quarto)

pronunciation: zz in mezzo, mezza and mezzogiorno is a voiced 'dz', held long: MED-dzo. In pizza it is a voiceless 'ts'.
Stress: sàbato (SA-ba-to), domènica (do-ME-ni-ca), but lunedì, martedì, mercoledì, giovedì, venerdì are stressed on the last syllable.

common_errors.why: Hours are plural except l'una, mezzogiorno and mezzanotte.
Alle shortens before the vowel of una.
Tra counts from now; in means how long something takes.

common_errors.wrong: Ci vediamo il sabato. (meaning this Saturday)
common_errors.why: Il sabato means every Saturday.

units.culture: Many shops, especially in small towns and the south, close for lunch (roughly 1 to 4 p.m.) and have one closing half-day a week, often Monday morning. Pharmacies take turns staying open at night and on holidays: the 'farmacia di turno' is posted on every pharmacy's door. Signs and timetables use the 24-hour clock, but people usually say 'alle quattro' rather than 'alle sedici'.
recycles: a1-06: C'è una farmacia qui vicino?
units.evidence: The learner asks and gives the time with sono le / è l'una, asks when a place opens or closes, understands dalle ... alle ..., and fixes a meeting time with alle ... or tra ... minuti.
sources: P1a U2 (telling the time, days of the week; lunedì vs il lunedì), U3 B (opening hours; real signs for pharmacy, bank, post office)
Proudfoot U5 (time: sono le / è l'una), U6 (a che ora, time words)
PREP (tra vs in; dalle ... alle ...)
EGSI ch.36 (che ore sono?)

units.title: At the market
units.can_do: Buy fruit, vegetables and cheese by weight, say how much you want, and finish the purchase.
functions: find your turn in a queue

frames.it: Buongiorno, chi è l'ultimo?
frames.en: Good morning, who's last in the queue?

grammar.explain: A weight or measure is joined to the food by di, with no article.

examples.en: a kilo of apples
half a kilo of courgettes
100 grams of ham

grammar.trap: 'Half a kilo' is mezzo chilo, with no un in front; and don't drop the di: 'mezzo chilo di pomodori'.

grammar.explain: Fruit and vegetables are usually asked for in the plural, and the article and adjectives agree.

examples.en: the peaches, the apricots
the ripe tomatoes

grammar.trap: -ca words add an h to keep the hard sound: pesca → pesche, albicocca → albicocche.

grammar.explain: Point with questi / queste for things near you and quelli / quelle lì for things further away, matching the gender of the food.

examples.en: These apples, please.
No, those over there.

grammar.trap: If you don't know the gender, point and say questi.

grammar.explain: In 'quanto ne vuole?' the ne means 'of it / of them'; you only need to understand it now and answer with an amount.

examples.en: How much would you like? — A kilo.

grammar.trap: You don't have to use ne yourself yet: 'Vorrei un chilo di pesche' is perfectly correct.

grammar.point: quanto vengono? for prices by weight
grammar.explain: At markets 'quanto vengono?' ('how much do they come to?') is a common way to ask a price.

examples.en: How much are the peaches?
How much is the pecorino?

grammar.trap: Plural produce takes vengono, one item viene, just like costano and costa.

vocabulary.en: cheese (central and southern word, often pecorino)
to be someone's turn (tocca a me); to touch
to be enough (basta così = that's all)

pronunciation: ch before e or i is a hard k: chilo (KEE-lo), pesche (PES-ke), albicocche (al-bi-KOK-ke). Without the h it softens: ciliegie (chee-LYEH-jeh).
Hold the doubles: etto, mezzo, zucchine, albicocca. 'Pèsca' (peach) has an open e; 'pésca' (fishing) a closed one, but context makes it clear.

common_errors.why: Mezzo takes no article.
A quantity needs di before the food.
Etto is a normal noun: plural etti.
You're buying several peaches: plural.

units.culture: At a market stall don't touch the produce: the stallholder picks it for you, or tell them what it's for (per oggi, per il sugo) and they'll choose. Where there's no visible queue, ask 'Chi è l'ultimo?' and remember who goes before you. In supermarkets you must wear the plastic gloves to pick fruit and weigh it yourself.
units.evidence: The learner finds their turn with chi è l'ultimo?, asks for amounts with chilo / etto + di, asks a price with quanto costano or quanto vengono, accepts or refuses a slightly different weight, and ends with basta così.
sources: P1B U8 C (deli counter: desidera? quanto ne vuole? due etti), moved down from A2
P2 U0 (tre etti)
Proudfoot U3 (availability and quantities at a market stall), U14 (ne vorrei un chilo)
P1B workbook (market vs supermarket)
Gap: queue etiquette (chi è l'ultimo, tocca a me) is in no book

grammar.explain: Non c'è says something is missing or not there.

examples.en: There's no hot water.
Is there a lift?

grammar.trap: No word for 'no' before the noun: 'non c'è acqua', not 'c'è nessuna acqua'.

grammar.explain: Funzionare ('to work', of machines) is used in the he/she/it form for one thing and funzionano for several.

examples.en: The washing machine isn't working.
The lights don't work.

grammar.trap: Machines don't 'lavorare': that verb is for people working.

grammar.point: qual è for 'what is' + a piece of information
grammar.explain: When you ask for a name, number, password or address, 'what is' is qual è.

examples.en: What's the password?

examples.it: Qual è il numero del tecnico?
examples.en: What's the repairman's number?

grammar.trap: 'Che cos'è' asks for a definition (What is it?). Written, qual è never has an apostrophe.

grammar.explain: Floors use ordinals with al: primo, secondo, terzo, quarto, quinto.

examples.en: I live on the first floor.

examples.it: È al quarto piano, senza ascensore.
examples.en: It's on the fourth floor, without a lift.

grammar.trap: The ground floor is il piano terra, so primo piano is what Americans call the second floor.

grammar.explain: Rooms of the house take in without an article.

examples.it: Il ferro da stiro è in cucina.
examples.en: The iron is in the kitchen.
I'm in the bathroom!

grammar.trap: Not 'nella cucina' for a normal statement; in cucina, in bagno, in camera, in soggiorno.

pronunciation: sc before e or i sounds like 'sh': ascensore (a-shen-SO-re). Hold the double cc in doccia (DOT-cha).
Funziona: z here is 'ts', and the stress is on -ziò-: fun-TSIO-na.

common_errors.why: Machines funzionano; people lavorano.
Asking for a piece of information is qual è.
Floors take al.
Acqua is feminine, so the adjective is calda.

units.culture: Each comune sorts rubbish differently, with its own calendar, colours and bins (plastica, carta, vetro, umido, indifferenziata). Putting the wrong bag out on the wrong day earns a sticker on the bag or a word from the neighbours, so ask early. Floors start from the piano terra (ground floor).
recycles: a1-08: days of the week (il martedì)
units.evidence: The learner says which floor they live on, asks how something works or where it is, reports a fault with non funziona / non c'è, and asks about the rubbish days, staying in Lei with the landlady.
sources: P1a U2 D (Lorenzo's new flat: floor, rooms, rent; al primo piano, al terzo piano senza ascensore), U3 C (furniture and where things are)
P1a U2 (ordinal numbers)
Proudfoot U4 (telling a house-sitter where things are), U10 (qual è)
EGSI ch.43 (che vs quale + essere)
Gap: no book has a landlady, repairs or rubbish rules

units.title: Small talk: likes, free time and the weather
units.can_do: Chat about what you like, what you do in your free time, and the weather, and ask the other person.
functions: agree or differ (anche a me / a me no)
situations: chatting with a regular at the counter

frames.it: Mi piacciono i carciofi.

frames.en: Me too! / Not me.

frames.en: Cold, isn't it?

grammar.point: mi piace + one thing or a verb; mi piacciono + several things
grammar.explain: In Italian the thing you like is the subject ('to me is pleasing'), so the verb agrees with it.

examples.en: I like pizza.
I like walking.
I like artichokes.

grammar.trap: Don't say 'io piaccio': that means 'I am liked'. Rebuild the English as 'to me is pleasing' first.

grammar.point: ti piace / Le piace; anche a me, neanche a me, a me no
grammar.explain: Ti piace asks a friend, Le piace asks someone you call Lei, and short answers keep the 'to me' shape.

examples.it: Ti piace il calcio? — Sì, e a te?
examples.en: Do you like football? — Yes, and you?
Do you like jazz? (Lei)

examples.it: Non mi piace il freddo. — Neanche a me.
examples.en: I don't like the cold. — Me neither.

grammar.trap: The reply to 'mi piace' is 'anche a me', not 'anche io'.

grammar.point: The present of regular verbs, all persons
grammar.explain: -are, -ere and -ire verbs have six endings, and some -ire verbs add -isc- in most forms.

examples.en: I walk, we walk, they walk
I read, you read, he/she reads
I prefer, you prefer, we prefer

grammar.trap: One Italian present covers 'I read', 'I'm reading' and 'I do read'; don't look for a separate -ing form.

grammar.explain: For hot and cold weather Italians say 'it makes': fa caldo, fa freddo.

examples.en: It's hot today.
The weather's nice.
It's raining.

grammar.trap: 'È freddo' describes a thing (the coffee is cold), not the weather. And 'ho freddo' means you feel cold.

vocabulary.en: to be pleasing (mi piace = I like)
not even, neither (neanche a me = me neither)

pronunciation: Third-person plurals are never stressed on the ending -ono/-ano: piàcciono (PYAT-cho-no), lèggono (LEG-go-no), cammìnano (kam-MEE-na-no).
ci and ce are 'ch': carciofi (kar-CHO-fee), piace (PYA-che), cucino (koo-CHEE-no).

common_errors.why: The thing liked is the subject; 'io piaccio' means 'I am liked'.
Several things take piacciono.
Weather uses fare.

common_errors.wrong: Mi piace molto il mare. — Anche io!
common_errors.why: The reply keeps the 'to me' shape of piacere.

units.culture: Food and the weather are the safest topics with anyone in Italy, and people will happily talk about both for a long time. 'Le piace qui?' is a chance to compliment the town; Italians are proud of where they live but often complain about it themselves.
recycles: a1-03: Sono qui per imparare l'italiano / Abito qui
units.evidence: The learner says what they like with mi piace / mi piacciono matched to the noun, asks back with ti piace or Le piace, answers with anche a me / a me no, names two or three free-time activities in the present, and makes a weather remark with fa caldo / fa freddo.
sources: P1a U2 A (free time interviews; mi piace / non mi piace ... e a te? as a chunk), U5 D (weather expressions)
Proudfoot U16 (piacere, anche a me / neanche a me), U6 (-ire verbs, present)
EGSI ch.19 (present covers -ing), ch.20 (fa freddo), ch.41 (piacere 'to be pleasing')
BG ch.5 (regular present, -isc- verbs)

grammar.point: Irregular present: andare, venire, fare, uscire
grammar.explain: These four everyday verbs don't follow the regular endings and must be learned as they are.

examples.it: vado, vai, va, andiamo, andate, vanno
examples.en: I go ... they go

examples.it: vengo, vieni, viene, veniamo, venite, vengono
examples.en: I come ... they come

examples.it: faccio, fai, fa; esco, esci, esce, usciamo
examples.en: I do/make ...; I go out ...

grammar.trap: Answer 'Vieni?' with 'Sì, vengo!': you 'come' towards the person or event you're invited to, not 'vado'.

grammar.explain: 'Can', 'want' and 'must' are followed directly by a verb in its basic form.

examples.en: I can't come.
Do you want to come with us?
I have to work.

grammar.trap: No 'to' after them: 'devo lavorare', not 'devo a lavorare'.

grammar.explain: Italians use the present tense for arranged plans, with a time word to show it's the future.

examples.en: Tomorrow I'm going to the seaside.
We're going out on Saturday.

grammar.trap: English 'I'm going to' is not 'vado a' + verb unless you're physically going somewhere: 'domani parto', not 'vado a partire'.

grammar.point: ti va? as a fixed invitation
grammar.explain: Ti va...? ('does it suit you?') is the friendliest way to suggest something, followed by a noun or di + verb.

examples.en: Fancy an ice cream?
Fancy going out tonight?

grammar.trap: Ti va is informal; with someone you call Lei, say 'Le va un caffè?'.

pronunciation: gli in vogliamo and voglio is one soft sound like the 'lli' in million: VO-lyo.
Stress: volentièri (vo-len-TYEH-ri), usciàmo (oo-SHA-mo), èsco (ES-ko). sc before i/e is 'sh' (uscire), before o is 'sk' (esco).

common_errors.why: Joining the people who invite you is venire.
Modal verbs take the infinitive directly.
Before a verb, ti va needs di.

common_errors.wrong: Domani io vado andare al mare.
common_errors.why: The present alone carries the plan.

units.culture: An invitation for 'un caffè' means five minutes standing at a bar, and the person who invites usually pays. Italians often decline gently ('magari un'altra volta') rather than say a flat no. Arriving ten or fifteen minutes late to a social plan is normal in much of Italy, though not for appointments or trains.
recycles: a1-08: A che ora? / alle sette / Ci vediamo
units.evidence: The learner invites with ti va...? or vieni...?, accepts with volentieri or declines with mi dispiace, non posso + a reason using devo + infinitive, offers an alternative, and fixes a place and time.
sources: P1a U2 B (invite, accept, refuse: Vieni con noi? Purtroppo non posso, devo studiare; Magari un'altra volta), U2 D (Sei libera domani pomeriggio? Ci vediamo domani alle 6?)
P1a U2 (irregular present andare, venire, uscire, fare; modal verbs)
Proudfoot U8 (potere), U13 (present for future), U18 (dovere)
EGSI ch.25 (present for near future)

lines.it: No, solo andata. Quant'è?
lines.en: No, one way. How much is it?

lines.speaker: clerk
lines.it: Sono otto euro e quaranta. Il regionale parte alle dieci e un quarto.
lines.en: That's eight euros forty. The regional train leaves at a quarter past ten.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Da che binario parte?
lines.en: Which platform does it leave from?

lines.speaker: clerk
lines.it: Dal binario cinque.
lines.en: From platform five.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Grazie, buona giornata!
lines.en: Thanks, have a good day!

model_exchanges.situation: Getting on a city bus

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Scusi, questo autobus va in centro?
lines.en: Excuse me, does this bus go to the centre?

lines.speaker: driver
lines.it: Sì, sì.
lines.en: Yes, it does.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Mi può dire dove devo scendere per il Duomo?
lines.en: Can you tell me where I should get off for the cathedral?

lines.speaker: driver
lines.it: Tra quattro fermate. Le dico io.
lines.en: In four stops. I'll tell you.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Grazie! Devo convalidare il biglietto?
lines.en: Thanks! Do I have to validate the ticket?

lines.speaker: driver
lines.it: Sì, lì, nella macchinetta gialla.
lines.en: Yes, there, in the yellow machine.

grammar.explain: Means of transport take in with no article, except on foot, which is a piedi.

examples.en: I'm going by train.
I'm coming by bus.
Let's walk.

grammar.trap: English 'by' is not per or con here: 'in treno', not 'per treno'.

grammar.explain: A ticket or a train 'to' a place uses per.

examples.en: a ticket to Rome
the train to Bologna

grammar.trap: Going to a city is 'vado a Roma', but a ticket or train for it is 'per Roma'.

grammar.explain: Devo ('I must / I have to') + a basic verb asks or says what you need to do.

examples.en: Where do I need to get off?
Do I have to change?

grammar.trap: In questions about what to do, Italian uses devo, not 'should' words: 'dove devo scendere?'.

grammar.point: si + verb as a chunk: dove si comprano?
grammar.explain: Si + verb means 'you / people' in general, and the verb agrees with the thing that follows.

examples.en: Where do you buy the ticket?
Where do you buy the tickets?

grammar.trap: Plural things make the verb plural: 'si comprano i biglietti'.

grammar.explain: Bisogna means 'you have to / it's necessary to', for everyone in general.

examples.en: You have to validate the ticket.
You have to change at Bologna.

grammar.trap: Bisogna never changes and is followed by a verb, not a noun.

pronunciation: gli in biglietto and biglietteria is the soft 'lly' sound, followed by a long tt: bi-LYET-to.
sc before i or e is 'sh': sciopero (SHO-pe-ro), scendere (SHEN-de-re).

common_errors.why: A ticket or train to a place takes per.
Transport takes in with no article.
With si the verb agrees with the plural noun.
On foot is a piedi; in piedi means standing.

units.culture: Paper tickets must be validated before you travel: on buses in the machine on board, for regional trains in the machines at the station. A regional ticket bought in the Trenitalia app or online is checked in automatically, so it needs no stamping. Inspectors fine on the spot, foreigners included. City bus tickets are sold at the tabaccheria, the newsstand or in an app, and many cities now take contactless cards at the gates. Transport strikes are announced in advance and usually leave guaranteed services at rush hour.
recycles: a1-08: A che ora parte? / alle dieci e un quarto / tra quattro fermate
a1-07: Dov'è la fermata? / in centro
units.evidence: The learner buys a ticket with per + destination, answers andata e ritorno?, asks the time and platform, checks whether a bus goes where they want, and asks where to get off; they understand 'in ritardo' and 'sciopero' when they hear them.
sources: P1a U2 culture (urban transport; buy tickets at tabaccheria, edicola, machines; validate at the start of the ride)
P1a U5 B (station dialogues: A che ora parte il prossimo treno per Firenze? Andata e ritorno? Da che binario parte?), workbook U5 ticket office
Proudfoot U18 (ticket office: bisogna prendere, bisogna pagare il supplemento)
P1B self-assessment (Solo andata?)
PREP (in + transport, a piedi)

units.title: Health basics and emergencies
units.can_do: Explain a simple health problem at the pharmacy, ask for something for it, and call for help in an emergency.
functions: say how long you've had it
situations: feeling ill in the first weeks

frames.it: Ho mal di testa.
frames.en: I've got a headache.

frames.it: Mi fa male la gola.
frames.en: My throat hurts.

frames.it: Ho la febbre da ieri.
frames.en: I've had a fever since yesterday.

frames.it: Ha qualcosa per il raffreddore?
frames.en: Have you got something for a cold?

frames.it: Cosa mi consiglia?
frames.en: What do you recommend?

frames.it: Sono allergico alla penicillina.
frames.en: I'm allergic to penicillin.
frames.note: A woman says allergica.

frames.it: Aiuto! Chiamate un'ambulanza!
frames.en: Help! Call an ambulance!

frames.it: Il numero per le emergenze è il 112.
frames.en: The emergency number is 112.

frames.it: Ho perso il portafoglio.
frames.en: I've lost my wallet.

model_exchanges.situation: At the pharmacy counter

lines.speaker: pharmacist
lines.it: Buongiorno, mi dica.
lines.en: Good morning, how can I help?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Buongiorno. Mi fa male la gola e ho un po' di tosse.
lines.en: Good morning. My throat hurts and I've got a bit of a cough.

lines.speaker: pharmacist
lines.it: Ha la febbre?
lines.en: Have you got a temperature?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: No, non ho la febbre. Cosa mi consiglia?
lines.en: No, I haven't got a temperature. What do you recommend?

lines.speaker: pharmacist
lines.it: Queste pastiglie, una ogni quattro ore. E uno sciroppo per la tosse.
lines.en: These lozenges, one every four hours. And a cough syrup.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Sono allergico alla penicillina.
lines.en: I'm allergic to penicillin.

lines.speaker: pharmacist
lines.it: Non c'è problema, non sono antibiotici.
lines.en: No problem, they're not antibiotics.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Grazie. Quant'è?
lines.en: Thanks. How much is it?

model_exchanges.situation: Someone is taken ill in the street

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Aiuto! Un signore sta male!
lines.en: Help! A man's been taken ill!

lines.speaker: passer-by
lines.it: Cosa succede?
lines.en: What's happening?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Non lo so. Chiamate un'ambulanza!
lines.en: I don't know. Call an ambulance!

lines.speaker: passer-by
lines.it: Chiamo il 112.
lines.en: I'm calling 112.

model_exchanges.situation: A lost wallet at a bar

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Scusi, ho perso il portafoglio. È nero.
lines.en: Excuse me, I've lost my wallet. It's black.

lines.speaker: barista
lines.it: Qui? No, mi dispiace.
lines.en: Here? No, I'm sorry.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Cosa faccio?
lines.en: What do I do?

lines.speaker: barista
lines.it: Vada dai carabinieri, sono qui vicino, in piazza.
lines.en: Go to the carabinieri, they're near here, in the square.

grammar.point: avere for states: ho mal di..., ho la febbre, ho freddo, ho fame
grammar.explain: Many physical states that English expresses with 'be' use avere ('have') in Italian.

examples.en: I've got a headache.
I've got a temperature.

examples.it: Ho freddo. / Ho fame. / Ho sete.
examples.en: I'm cold. / I'm hungry. / I'm thirsty.

grammar.trap: Not 'sono fame' or 'sono freddo': think 'I have hunger', 'I have cold'. Note mal di (not male di).

grammar.point: mi fa male + one thing, mi fanno male + several (chunk)
grammar.explain: 'X hurts me' is mi fa male X, and the verb agrees with the part that hurts.

examples.en: My back hurts.
My feet hurt.

grammar.trap: Use the article, not 'my': 'mi fa male la gola', not 'la mia gola fa male'.

grammar.explain: For a symptom you still have, say how long with da and the present tense.

examples.it: Ho la tosse da tre giorni.
examples.en: I've had a cough for three days.
I've had a temperature since yesterday.

grammar.trap: Not the past: 'ho avuto la febbre per due giorni' means it's over.

grammar.point: chiamate! and ho perso as chunks
grammar.explain: Chiamate! is an urgent command to everyone around you, and ho perso ('I've lost') can be used now, before the past tense is taught.

examples.en: Call a doctor!
I've lost my keys.

grammar.trap: To one person you know, say chiama!; to a stranger, chiami!; to a crowd, chiamate!

pronunciation: Hold the double consonants, which carry the meaning: tosse (cough), febbre, raffreddore, sciroppo. Febbre has a long bb: FEB-bre.
sc before i is 'sh': sciroppo (shee-ROP-po). In schiena, sch is 'sk': SKYEH-na.

common_errors.why: Physical states take avere.
In this fixed phrase male shortens to mal.
Several things hurting take fanno.
Italian says 'to me hurts the head', with the article, not 'my'.

common_errors.wrong: Ho la febbre per due giorni. (still ill)
common_errors.right: Ho la febbre da due giorni.
common_errors.why: Something still going on takes da + present.

units.culture: The pharmacy (green cross) is the first stop for minor illness: pharmacists give real advice and sell many medicines without a prescription, though antibiotics always need a ricetta. 112 is the single emergency number everywhere in Italy; 118 still reaches an ambulance directly in many regions. A&E (pronto soccorso) sorts patients by urgency, so minor problems can mean a long wait.
recycles: a1-02: Non ho capito / Può ripetere?
a1-06: Ha qualcosa per ...? / C'è una farmacia qui vicino?
a1-08: farmacia di turno, opening hours
units.evidence: At a pharmacy the learner names a symptom with ho mal di / mi fa male / ho la febbre, says since when with da, asks for something or for advice, and mentions an allergy; in an emergency they can call for help and say what they've lost.
units.review: after 1, 3 and 7 conversations, then before any trip
sources: Gap: no book teaches health at A1 (P1a §5, P1B §5, Proudfoot §5)
Vocabulary from P2 U6 (febbre, tosse) and P3 U17
P1a U3 culture (112, European emergency number)
EGSI ch.20 (avere for states: ho fame, ho freddo)
Proudfoot U8 (Non posso mangiare le fragole, perché sono allergica), U11 (da + present)

units.title: What you did: the first past
units.can_do: Say what you did yesterday or at the weekend, and ask someone what they did.
functions: tell a short sequence of events
situations: someone who remembers you asks about yesterday
telling a neighbour about a day out

frames.it: Cosa hai fatto ieri? / Cosa ha fatto ieri?
frames.en: What did you do yesterday? (tu / Lei)

frames.it: Cosa hai fatto di bello nel fine settimana?
frames.en: Did you do anything nice at the weekend?

frames.it: Sono andato al mercato e ho comprato le pesche.
frames.en: I went to the market and bought peaches.
frames.note: A woman says sono andata.

frames.it: Ho mangiato in una trattoria buonissima.
frames.en: I ate at a really good trattoria.

frames.it: Sabato sono stata a Siena.
frames.en: On Saturday I went to Siena.
frames.note: Said by a woman; a man says sono stato.

frames.it: Prima abbiamo fatto un giro, poi siamo andati a cena.
frames.en: First we went for a stroll, then we went out to dinner.

frames.it: Due giorni fa ho visto un concerto in piazza.
frames.en: Two days ago I saw a concert in the square.

frames.it: Che bello! / Peccato!
frames.en: How lovely! / What a shame!

frames.it: Com'è andato il fine settimana?
frames.en: How was your weekend?

model_exchanges.situation: Monday morning at the bar (tu)

lines.speaker: barista
lines.it: Ciao! Cosa hai fatto di bello nel fine settimana?
lines.en: Hi! Did you do anything nice at the weekend?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Sabato sono andata a Siena con un'amica.
lines.en: On Saturday I went to Siena with a friend.

lines.speaker: barista
lines.it: Che bello! E domenica?
lines.en: How lovely! And Sunday?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Domenica sono stata a casa. Ho cucinato e ho letto.
lines.en: On Sunday I stayed at home. I cooked and read.

lines.speaker: barista
lines.it: Brava! Io invece ho lavorato tutto il giorno.
lines.en: Good for you! I worked all day, though.

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Peccato!
lines.en: What a shame!

model_exchanges.situation: An older neighbour asks about yesterday (Lei)

lines.speaker: neighbour
lines.it: Buongiorno! Cosa ha fatto ieri?
lines.en: Good morning! What did you do yesterday?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Sono andato al mercato e ho comprato le pesche. Poi ho mangiato in una trattoria buonissima.
lines.en: I went to the market and bought peaches. Then I ate at a really good trattoria.

lines.speaker: neighbour
lines.it: Quale?
lines.en: Which one?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Da Mario, vicino alla piazza.
lines.en: Da Mario, near the square.

lines.speaker: neighbour
lines.it: Ah, Da Mario! Lì si mangia bene.
lines.en: Ah, Da Mario! The food's good there.

model_exchanges.situation: Telling a friend about an evening out (tu)

lines.speaker: friend
lines.it: Hai visto il concerto in piazza?
lines.en: Did you see the concert in the square?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Sì, due giorni fa! Prima abbiamo fatto un giro, poi siamo andati al concerto.
lines.en: Yes, two days ago! First we went for a stroll, then we went to the concert.

lines.speaker: friend
lines.it: E dopo?
lines.en: And after that?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Alla fine abbiamo mangiato una pizza.
lines.en: In the end we had a pizza.

grammar.point: passato prossimo = avere or essere + past participle
grammar.explain: The everyday past is two words: the present of avere or essere plus a past participle, and it covers both 'I did' and 'I have done'.

examples.en: I ate. / I've eaten.
Did you see the concert?
I went to the market.

grammar.trap: There's no 'did' in Italian questions or negatives: 'Cosa hai fatto?', 'Non ho visto niente'.

grammar.explain: Regular participles end in -ato (-are verbs), -uto (-ere) and -ito (-ire), but many everyday ones are irregular and learned by heart.

examples.en: eaten, had, slept
done, seen, taken, read
drunk, said, been

grammar.trap: Don't regularise the irregulars: 'preso', not 'prenduto'; 'fatto', not 'faciuto'.

grammar.point: essere with movement and staying, and the participle agrees
grammar.explain: Andare, venire, tornare, arrivare, uscire and stare take essere, and then the participle ends in -o, -a, -i or -e to match the subject.

examples.en: I went (man / woman)
We went out at eight.
On Saturday I went to Siena. (woman)

grammar.trap: 'Ho andato' is the classic English-speaker error: verbs of going and coming take sono. Sono stato/a also means 'I went to (a place)'.

grammar.explain: Ieri, sabato scorso and due giorni fa place the event; prima, poi and alla fine order it.

examples.en: Last night I went out.

examples.it: Sabato scorso ho visto una mostra.
examples.en: Last Saturday I saw an exhibition.

examples.it: Prima abbiamo mangiato, poi siamo andati al cinema.
examples.en: First we ate, then we went to the cinema.

grammar.trap: 'Ago' comes after the time: 'due giorni fa', not 'fa due giorni'. 'Last' is scorso and agrees: la settimana scorsa.

vocabulary.en: to go for a stroll, a wander

pronunciation: The h in ho, hai, ha and hanno is silent: ho visto sounds like 'o visto', and hanno sounds just like anno.
Keep double consonants long in participles: fatto, detto, letto, messo. Fato (fate) and fatto (done) are different words.

common_errors.why: Andare takes essere.
Mangiare takes avere.

common_errors.wrong: Sabato sono andato a Siena. (said by a woman)
common_errors.why: With essere the participle agrees with the speaker.

common_errors.wrong: Fa due giorni ho visto un concerto.
common_errors.right: Due giorni fa ho visto un concerto.
common_errors.why: Fa follows the length of time.
A finished event in the past needs the passato prossimo.

units.culture: 'Com'è andato il fine settimana?' and 'Cosa hai fatto di bello?' are a Monday ritual at the bar, at work and on the stairs. People who know you will remember what you told them and ask about it, and they expect a short, lively answer with a reaction ('Che bello!', 'Peccato!'), not a long report.
recycles: a1-11: mi piace / leggo, cammino, cucino
a1-12: andare, venire, uscire, fare; il fine settimana
a1-07: in piazza, vicino alla piazza
units.evidence: Asked about yesterday or the weekend, the learner tells two or three events in order with prima / poi / alla fine, chooses sono for andare, stare, uscire and tornare and ho for the rest, makes the participle agree with their own gender, and asks the question back.
units.review: after 1, 3 and 7 conversations, then each Monday for a month
sources: P1a U4 A (Monday-morning weekend chat: Come hai passato il fine settimana? Che cosa hai fatto di bello?), U4 B (the police interview: narrating a day), workbook U4
Proudfoot U11 (passato prossimo; essere verbs; fa, scorso)
EGSI ch.23 (passato prossimo, auxiliary choice, agreement)

units.title: Family and the people in your life
units.can_do: Talk about your family and the people in your life, and describe what someone looks like and is like.
situations: showing family photos to a neighbour
explaining who is coming to visit
sorting out whose coat or keys are whose after dinner

frames.it: Ha figli? — Sì, un figlio e una figlia.
frames.en: Do you have children? — Yes, a son and a daughter.
frames.note: To a friend: Hai figli?

frames.it: Mia figlia vive all'estero, negli Stati Uniti.
frames.en: My daughter lives abroad, in the United States.
frames.note: in + country; a plural country takes the article: negli Stati Uniti, nei Paesi Bassi.

frames.it: I miei genitori vengono a trovarmi a maggio.
frames.en: My parents are coming to visit me in May.
frames.note: venire a trovare = to come and visit someone.

frames.it: Questa è la mia compagna.
frames.en: This is my partner.
frames.note: il mio compagno for a man. A partner isn't a relative, so the article stays.

frames.it: Quanti nipoti ha?
frames.en: How many grandchildren do you have?
frames.note: nipote = grandchild and also niece or nephew.

frames.it: Com'è tua sorella?
frames.en: What's your sister like?
frames.note: Com'è? = what is she like; Come sta? = how is she (health).

frames.it: È alta, bionda e molto simpatica.
frames.en: She's tall, blonde and very nice.

frames.it: Di chi è questa borsa? — È mia.
frames.en: Whose bag is this? — It's mine.

model_exchanges.situation: showing photos on your phone to a neighbour (Lei)

lines.speaker: vicina
lines.it: Che belle foto! Chi sono?
lines.en: What lovely photos! Who are they?

lines.it: Questa è mia figlia, e questo è mio figlio con sua moglie.

lines.speaker: vicina

lines.speaker: vicina

lines.en: Yes, a little granddaughter of three. My children are coming to visit me in May.

lines.speaker: vicina
lines.it: Che bello! Così li conosco!
lines.en: How lovely! Then I'll get to meet them!

model_exchanges.situation: waiting for a friend at a bar (tu, you're a regular)

lines.speaker: barista
lines.it: Aspetti qualcuno?
lines.en: Are you waiting for someone?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Sì, una mia amica. È alta, ha i capelli corti e gli occhi verdi.
lines.en: Yes, a friend of mine. She's tall, she has short hair and green eyes.

lines.speaker: barista
lines.it: E com'è? Simpatica?
lines.en: And what's she like? Nice?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Molto simpatica, e un po' matta!
lines.en: Very nice, and a bit crazy!

lines.speaker: amico
lines.it: Di chi sono queste chiavi?

lines.speaker: newcomer
lines.it: Sono mie, grazie!
lines.en: They're mine, thanks!
