points.point: quello che / ciò che as a subject
points.explain: Quello che / ciò che can start a sentence as its subject: quello che mi colpisce è la luce.
points.trap: English 'what strikes me' tempts cosa mi colpisce, which is a question.

points.point: ne in 'a quanto ne so'
points.explain: A quanto ne so means 'as far as I know', with ne standing for 'about it'.
points.trap: The ne is required; a quanto so sounds incomplete.

points.point: indefinites and proprio (ognuno... i propri; qualunque + subjunctive)
points.explain: Proprio replaces suo after general subjects (ognuno ha i propri difetti), and qualunque + noun takes the subjunctive.
points.trap: Ognuno ha i suoi difetti is also heard, but i propri avoids ambiguity.

points.point: combined pronouns with fare (gliel'ho fatto notare)
points.explain: Pronouns go before fare, not the infinitive: gliel'ho fatto notare, me lo faccia sapere.
points.trap: Attaching them to the infinitive (ho fatto notarglielo) is wrong.

points.point: nessuno / nessun / alcun
points.explain: Nessun/nessuna and alcun/alcuna before a singular noun mean 'no / not any': non c'è alcun problema.
points.trap: They take singular nouns only (nessun bambino, not nessuni bambini).

points.point: il quale / il cui
points.explain: Il quale (agreeing with its noun) is a formal alternative to che/cui; il cui means 'whose', agreeing with the thing owned: il comune, il cui bilancio...
points.trap: Il cui agrees with what follows (le cui finestre), not with the owner.

points.point: ci and ne idioms (ci tengo, non ne posso più, ne vale la pena)
points.explain: Ci and ne appear in fixed expressions: ci tengo (it matters to me), non ne posso più (I can't take it any more), ne vale la pena (it's worth it).
points.trap: Translating word for word loses the meaning.

points.point: colui che / coloro che / ciò che
points.explain: Colui che / coloro che (he who / those who) are formal equivalents of chi and quelli che.
points.trap: Too formal for chat; chi is enough in speech.

groups.name: Present indicative (essere, avere, stare, regular and irregular verbs, modals)

points.point: stare for how you are: sto bene (trap: not sono bene)
points.explain: To say how you are, Italian uses stare: sto bene, sta bene?
points.trap: 'I am well' pushes English speakers to say sono bene, which is wrong.

points.point: può + infinitive as a fixed polite request (può ripetere?)
points.explain: Può followed by a verb in its dictionary form asks a stranger politely to do something: può ripetere?
points.trap: English adds 'could you... please'; Italian needs no extra word, but say per favore and use può (Lei), not puoi, with strangers.

points.point: essere in the present (sono, sei, è); subject pronouns usually dropped
points.explain: Essere means 'to be' (sono, sei, è, siamo, siete, sono) and you normally leave out io, tu, lui because the verb ending shows who.
points.trap: English needs 'I', 'he', 'it'; saying io sono every time sounds heavy, and there is no word for 'it' as a subject (è bello).

points.point: -are verbs for io / tu / Lei: abito, abiti, abita; lavoro
points.explain: Regular -are verbs drop -are and add -o for io, -i for tu and -a for lui/lei/Lei.
points.trap: The stress stays on the stem (àbito, not abìto), and the Lei form is the same as 'he/she', not the tu form.

points.point: da + present for 'have been … for' (sono qui da tre settimane; trap: not 'sono stato qui per')
points.explain: For something that started in the past and is still going on, Italian uses the present tense with da: sono in Italia da un mese.
points.trap: English uses 'have been'; translating it as sono stato qui per tre settimane means you're no longer here.

points.point: prendere for food and drink: prendo, prendi, prende
points.explain: Italians 'take' food and drink: prendo un caffè means 'I'll have a coffee'.
points.trap: Don't translate 'have' as avere when ordering (ho un caffè means you're holding one).

points.point: costa with one thing, costano with several
points.explain: The verb agrees with the thing that costs: quanto costa il pane? but quanto costano le pesche?
points.trap: English 'how much is/are' hides the plural; learners say quanto costa questi.

points.point: posso + infinitive (posso pagare?)
points.explain: Posso followed by a verb in the infinitive asks permission or possibility: posso pagare con la carta?
points.trap: There is no 'to' before the second verb: posso pagare, not posso a pagare.

points.point: c'è / ci sono; avete...?
points.explain: C'è (there is) is used with one thing and ci sono (there are) with several; in a shop, avete...? asks if they have it.
points.trap: English 'is there' often comes out as è, which just means 'it is'.

points.point: the present for near plans (torno, ci vediamo)
points.explain: Italians use the present tense for arranged or near-future plans: domani torno alle sei.
points.trap: There's no need for 'going to' or 'will'; andare a means physically going somewhere.

points.point: quanto vengono? = how much are they?
points.explain: At markets quanto vengono? (or quanto viene al chilo?) is a common way to ask the price.
points.trap: Venire normally means 'come', so the price meaning surprises learners.

points.point: c'è / non c'è recycled
points.explain: Non c'è means 'there isn't': non c'è acqua calda.
points.trap: English 'there's no...' leads to c'è no; Italian puts non in front: non c'è.

points.point: funziona / non funziona (3rd person singular)
points.explain: Funziona (it works) and non funziona (it doesn't work) describe machines and services; funzionano for several.
points.trap: Use the 3rd person: the shower works = la doccia funziona; lavorare is only for people working.

points.point: the present of regular verbs, all persons (-are, -ere, -ire, and -isc: preferisco)
points.explain: Regular verbs follow three patterns (-are, -ere, -ire), and many -ire verbs insert -isc- (preferisco, capisci, finisce) except for noi and voi.
points.trap: The loro form is stressed early (pàrlano, not parlàno), and the present also covers English '-ing' and 'do'.

points.point: irregular present: andare, venire, fare, uscire
points.explain: Andare (vado), venire (vengo), fare (faccio) and uscire (esco) are irregular and must be learned by heart.
points.trap: Andare is 'go there', venire 'come here / come with the speaker': vieni con noi?, not vai con noi?

points.point: potere, volere, dovere + infinitive
points.explain: Potere (can), volere (want) and dovere (must) are followed directly by an infinitive: devo lavorare.
points.trap: No 'to' after them; and 'can' meaning 'know how' is sapere (so nuotare).

points.point: the present for plans (domani vado) — the future tense waits for A2
points.explain: Plans are told in the present with a time word: domani vado al mare.
points.trap: 'I'm going to go' isn't vado ad andare; just say vado.

points.point: devo + infinitive
points.explain: Devo + infinitive says what you have to do: devo scendere qui.
points.trap: 'Have to' is not ho da (regional) or ho a; use devo.

points.point: avere for states: ho mal di..., ho la febbre, ho freddo, ho fame (trap: not sono fame)
points.explain: Hunger, thirst, cold, heat, fear, age and aches use avere: ho fame, ho trent'anni, ho mal di testa.
points.trap: English 'I am hungry/cold/30' produces sono fame, sono freddo, sono trenta.

points.point: da + present recycled: ho la febbre da ieri
points.explain: Da + time with the present says how long or since when: ho la tosse da tre giorni.
points.trap: English 'I've had' leads to ho avuto; use the present.

points.point: stare + gerund only for what's happening now (mi sto abituando) — trap: Italian uses the plain present far more than English -ing
points.explain: Sto + gerund (sto mangiando) is only for an action in progress right now; the simple present covers most English '-ing'.
points.trap: 'I'm working in Rome this year' is lavoro a Roma, not sto lavorando, and stare + gerund never expresses the future.

points.point: the present still fine for near plans
points.explain: For arranged plans the present is as natural as the future: a Ferragosto vado al mare.
points.trap: Overusing the future for every plan sounds bookish.

points.point: avere ragione / torto
points.explain: Hai ragione = you're right; ha torto = he's wrong.
points.trap: English 'be right' becomes sei giusto, which is wrong for people.

points.point: da + present for symptoms
points.explain: Da + time with the present tells the doctor how long a symptom has lasted: ho mal di testa da due giorni.
points.trap: 'I've had a headache for two days' is not ho avuto per due giorni.

points.point: da + present for 'hasn't worked since'
points.explain: Non funziona da ieri = it hasn't worked since yesterday.
points.trap: English perfect 'hasn't worked' tempts non ha funzionato da.

points.point: sono X che + present for duration
points.explain: Sono due settimane che aspetto = I've been waiting for two weeks; è un anno che for singular.
points.trap: English perfect 'I've been waiting' leads to ho aspettato.

points.point: irregular presents refined (riempire, sciogliere, valere, tacere)
points.explain: Some verbs have irregular presents: riempio, sciolgo, valgo, taccio.
points.trap: Regularising them (riempisco, sciogo) is common.

groups.name: Impersonal and "backwards" verbs (piacere, servire, bisogna, ci vuole, fare for weather)

points.point: mi piace + one thing or a verb, mi piacciono + several: the thing liked is the subject
points.explain: Piacere works 'backwards': the thing you like is the subject, so mi piace il caffè but mi piacciono i carciofi.
points.trap: English 'I like' makes learners say io piaccio or mi piace i carciofi.

points.point: weather with fare: fa caldo, fa freddo (trap: not è freddo)
points.explain: Weather uses fare: fa caldo, fa freddo, fa bel tempo; rain and snow have their own verbs (piove, nevica).
points.trap: 'It's cold' is fa freddo; è freddo describes a thing (il caffè è freddo).

points.point: ti va? as a fixed invitation
points.explain: Ti va (di)...? means 'do you fancy...?': ti va un caffè?
points.trap: It's not about going anywhere; the answer is sì, mi va / no, non mi va.

points.point: bisogna + infinitive, understood
points.explain: Bisogna + infinitive means 'you have to / it's necessary to': bisogna convalidare il biglietto.
points.trap: Bisogna never changes and has no subject; it's not 'bisogno'.

points.point: mi fa male + one thing, mi fanno male + several (chunk)
points.explain: Mi fa male la gola = my throat hurts; with plural body parts use mi fanno male (gli occhi).
points.trap: The body part is the subject and takes the article (la gola), not a possessive (la mia gola).

points.point: piacere for others: gli piace, le piacciono
points.explain: To say someone else likes something, use gli (him/them) or le (her) + piace/piacciono, or a + name: a Marco piace il vino.
points.trap: Lui piace il vino is wrong; it's gli piace or a lui piace.

points.point: stare bene a qualcuno: mi sta, ti sta
points.explain: Clothes 'stay well to' someone: mi sta bene? ti sta benissimo!
points.trap: The garment is the subject; 'it fits me' isn't mi fitta or lo sto bene.

points.point: Le dispiace se...?
points.explain: Le dispiace se...? (ti dispiace se...?) asks 'do you mind if...?'.
points.trap: Answering 'no' means 'go ahead': No, si figuri; sì means you do mind.

points.point: mi sembra / mi pare + adjective
points.explain: Mi sembra + adjective gives a soft opinion: mi sembra caro (it seems expensive to me).
points.trap: The thing is the subject: le scarpe mi sembrano care (plural).

points.point: serve / servono agree with what's needed
points.explain: Serve (it's needed) agrees with the thing: serve il passaporto, servono due foto.
points.trap: English 'you need' leads to tu servi; the person goes in the indirect pronoun (mi servono).

points.point: bisogna / serve / occorre + infinitive or noun; basta + noun
points.explain: Bisogna + infinitive, serve/occorre + noun or infinitive and basta + noun all express what's needed or enough.
points.trap: Bisogna never takes a noun (bisogna il passaporto is wrong: serve il passaporto).

points.point: ci vuole / ci vogliono for time and things needed
points.explain: Ci vuole (singular) and ci vogliono (plural) say how much time or what is needed: ci vogliono due settimane.
points.trap: The verb agrees with what's needed; for the time a person takes, use metterci (ci metto un'ora).

points.point: mi sta simpatico / simpatica (the indirect pronoun again)
points.explain: Mi sta simpatico/a means 'I like him/her' as a person; the person is the subject.
points.trap: Mi piace about a person can suggest attraction; mi sta simpatico is safer.

points.point: chiamarsi for io / tu / Lei as a chunk (mi chiamo, ti chiami, si chiama)
points.explain: Mi chiamo... (literally 'I call myself') is how you give your name; ti chiami for tu, si chiama for Lei.
points.trap: Learners say il mio nome è, which is correct but stiff; and it's come ti chiami?, never cosa ti chiami?

points.point: reflexive verbs in the present: mi alzo, ti trovi, si trova
points.explain: Many daily-routine verbs take mi, ti, si, ci, vi, si before the verb: mi alzo alle sette.
points.trap: The pronoun can't be dropped (alzo alle sette is wrong), and body parts take the article (mi lavo i denti).

points.point: reflexives in the past take essere, and the participle agrees (mi sono perso / persa)
points.explain: Reflexive verbs always use essere in the past, so the participle agrees: mi sono alzata (said by a woman).
points.trap: English 'I have' leads to mi ho alzato.

points.point: abituarsi a
points.explain: Abituarsi a + noun or infinitive means 'to get used to': mi sto abituando agli orari.
points.trap: The preposition is a, and the verb is reflexive: not abituo or abituarsi di.

points.point: ricordarsi di
points.explain: Ricordarsi di + noun or infinitive means 'to remember': ti ricordi di me?
points.trap: Ricordare (without si) is also possible but takes no di; mixing them gives ricordo di.

points.point: farsi male a + body part (past with essere)
points.explain: Farsi male a + body part means 'to hurt your...': mi sono fatto male al ginocchio.
points.trap: It's reflexive, so the past uses essere; and a + article, not 'my' (al ginocchio).

points.point: with reflexives: me ne sono dimenticato
points.explain: Reflexive verbs combine with ne as me ne, te ne, se ne: me ne sono dimenticato.
points.trap: The past uses essere because the verb is reflexive.

points.point: pronominal verbs: farcela, cavarsela, andarsene, prendersela
points.explain: Some verbs carry fixed pronouns that change their meaning: farcela (to manage), cavarsela (to get by), andarsene (to leave), prendersela (to take offence).
points.trap: The pronouns conjugate (ce la faccio, me la cavo, se n'è andato) and can't be dropped.

points.point: sentirsi + adjective
points.explain: Sentirsi + adjective describes how you feel: mi sento a casa, mi sentivo straniero.
points.trap: Not mi sento come un straniero; the adjective agrees with you.

points.point: pronominal idioms: avercela con, farcela, mettercela tutta, vedersela brutta, prendersela, farsene una ragione
points.explain: Verbs with fixed pronouns form idioms: avercela con qualcuno (be angry with), farsene una ragione (accept it).
points.trap: The pronouns conjugate and agree in compound tenses (ce l'ho messa tutta).

points.point: ho capito / non ho capito as fixed past forms, ahead of the past tense
points.explain: Ho capito (I understand / I've got it) and non ho capito (I didn't understand) are learned as set phrases before the past tense is taught.
points.trap: Italians say non ho capito where English says 'I don't understand'; capisco is also fine but less common in the moment.

points.point: passato prossimo = avere or essere + past participle
points.explain: The everyday past is the present of avere or essere plus a past participle: ho mangiato, sono andato.
points.trap: It translates both 'I ate' and 'I have eaten'; don't look for a separate simple past.

points.point: regular participles -ato, -uto, -ito; common irregulars fatto, visto, preso, bevuto, detto, stato
points.explain: Participles end in -ato (-are), -uto (-ere) and -ito (-ire), but many common verbs are irregular: fatto, visto, preso, detto.
points.trap: Regularising irregular verbs (prenduto, faciuto) is natural but wrong.

points.point: essere with andare, venire, tornare, arrivare, uscire, stare, and the participle agrees (andato / andata)
points.explain: Verbs of movement and staying take essere, and then the participle agrees with the subject: Maria è andata.
points.trap: English always uses 'have', so learners say ho andato; a woman says sono andata.

points.point: the participle agrees after lo / la / li / le (l'ho presa) — recognise
points.explain: After lo, la, li, le, the past participle agrees with the pronoun: la pasta? l'ho comprata.
points.trap: English has no agreement; listen for the ending to know what's being talked about.

points.point: the participle doesn't agree with an indirect pronoun (le ho dato)
points.explain: With gli, le and other indirect pronouns the participle stays masculine singular: le ho telefonato.
points.trap: Don't over-apply the lo/la agreement rule (le ho telefonata is wrong).

points.point: in the past with agreement (gliel'ho data)
points.explain: In compound tenses the participle agrees with lo/la/li/le inside a combined pronoun: la chiave? te l'ho data.
points.trap: The elision (gliel'ho) hides the gender, so the participle ending carries it.

points.point: era (past of essere) as a chunk
points.explain: Era (it was) describes how something was: era tutto buonissimo.
points.trap: For a description use era, not è stato, in most everyday cases.

points.point: imperfetto forms: -avo / -evo / -ivo; ero, facevo, bevevo, dicevo
points.explain: The imperfect is built on the infinitive stem with -avo, -evo or -ivo; essere (ero) is the main irregular, and fare, bere, dire use old stems.
points.trap: The stress falls on the ending in noi/voi (andavàmo) and early in loro (andàvano).

points.point: imperfetto for background, habits and description; passato prossimo for events (trap: English 'went' gives no clue)
points.explain: Use the imperfect for what used to happen, what was going on and what things were like, and the passato prossimo for single completed events.
points.trap: English 'went' or 'was' fits both; 'used to' and 'was -ing' point to the imperfect.

points.point: volevo... as a polite imperfect
points.explain: Volevo + infinitive or noun is a polite way to start a request: volevo chiederLe una cosa.
points.trap: It sounds past to English ears, but it means 'I wanted to / I'd like to' right now.

points.point: passato prossimo and imperfetto together in an explanation
points.explain: When explaining a problem, the background is imperfect (non funzionava) and the events are passato prossimo (ho chiamato il tecnico).
points.trap: Putting everything in one tense blurs what happened and what the situation was.

points.point: imperfetto and passato prossimo in a complaint
points.explain: Describe the state of things in the imperfect (la camera era sporca) and what happened in the passato prossimo (nessuno ci ha aiutato).
points.trap: Using passato prossimo for descriptions (la camera è stata sporca) sounds wrong.

points.point: potevi / dovevi + infinitive as a reproach
points.explain: Potevi dirmelo! (you could have told me) uses the imperfect of potere/dovere as a reproach.
points.trap: English 'could have told' tempts potresti avere detto.

points.point: imperfetto in childhood narration
points.explain: Childhood memories are told in the imperfect: da bambino leggevo sotto le coperte.
points.trap: English 'would' (habit) must become the imperfect, not the conditional.

groups.name: Trapassato prossimo, passato remoto, trapassato remoto

points.point: trapassato prossimo (era già partito, avevo dimenticato)
points.explain: The trapassato (avevo/ero + participle) is for something that had already happened before another past event.
points.trap: English often lets 'went' stand for 'had gone'; Italian needs the trapassato.

points.point: passato remoto for recognition (fu, ebbe, nacque, morì, costruirono, dipinse)
points.explain: The passato remoto is the past of history, books and guides (fu costruito, nacque nel 1475); in much of the south it's also spoken.
points.trap: Many forms are irregular and look unrelated to the infinitive (nacque from nascere, dipinse from dipingere).

points.point: passato remoto in narration (recognise; a few set forms produced)
points.explain: In art and history talk, the passato remoto narrates distant events (fu completato, dipinse); a few third-person forms are worth saying.
points.trap: Don't use it for your own recent past, except in parts of the south where people speak that way.

points.point: passato remoto produced in narrative
points.explain: Historical narrative uses the passato remoto for events: Garibaldi sbarcò a Marsala nel 1860.
points.trap: Mixing it with the passato prossimo in the same story sounds odd; pick one narrative tense.

points.point: trapassato remoto (dopo che ebbero firmato) — written and formal
points.explain: The trapassato remoto (ebbe firmato) appears after dopo che, appena, quando in formal narrative.
points.trap: In speech the trapassato prossimo or a past infinitive replaces it.

points.point: mixing narrative tenses
points.explain: A story mixes passato remoto or prossimo for events, imperfect for background and trapassato for what came before.
points.trap: Keep the same narrative tense for the main events.

points.point: futuro semplice, regular and irregular (andrò, sarò, avrò, farò, verrò, potrò)
points.explain: The future adds -ò, -ai, -à, -emo, -ete, -anno to the infinitive minus -e (-are verbs change a to e: parlerò); common verbs shorten the stem (andrò, avrò, verrò).
points.trap: There's no 'will'; the ending carries the meaning, and the stress is on the last syllable (andrò).

points.point: the future for guesses about now: sarà chiuso, saranno le otto
points.explain: The future also expresses a guess about the present: sarà chiuso (it must be closed).
points.trap: English uses 'must be / probably'; hearing sarà, learners think it's about tomorrow.

points.point: futuro anteriore after quando / appena / dopo che (understand)
points.explain: The future perfect (avrò finito, sarà arrivato) marks something that will be finished before another future action, or a guess about the past.
points.trap: English uses 'have done' after 'when'; Italian uses the future perfect (quando avrò finito).

points.point: the concessive future (sarà anche vero)
points.explain: The future can concede a point before disagreeing: sarà anche vero, ma...
points.trap: It's not about the future; it means 'it may well be'.

points.point: vorrei as a fixed polite phrase (the conditional comes at A2)
points.explain: Vorrei means 'I'd like' and is the polite way to ask for anything in a shop or bar.
points.trap: Voglio (I want) sounds blunt when ordering; save it for friends.

points.point: condizionale presente: the future stem + -ei, -esti, -ebbe... (vorrei, potrei, dovrei, prenderei, sarebbe)
points.explain: The conditional uses the future's stem with -ei, -esti, -ebbe, -emmo, -este, -ebbero.
points.trap: Don't confuse -emmo (conditional) with -emo (future): andremmo vs andremo.

points.point: uses: polite requests, wishes, advice, softening
points.explain: The conditional asks politely (potrebbe...?), wishes (mi piacerebbe), advises (dovresti) and softens (direi).
points.trap: 'Would' meaning 'used to' is the imperfect, not the conditional.

points.point: polite conditional (potrebbe controllare?)
points.explain: Potrebbe + infinitive makes a complaint into a polite request.
points.trap: Può is acceptable, but potrebbe keeps a complaint courteous.

points.point: potrei + infinitive
points.explain: Potrei + infinitive asks politely for yourself: potrei parlare con...?
points.trap: Posso is fine too, but potrei is the polite norm on the phone.

points.point: condizionale passato (avrei dovuto, sarei venuto)
points.explain: The past conditional (avrei/sarei + participle) is for what would have happened or should have been done: avrei dovuto prenotare.
points.trap: 'I should have' is avrei dovuto, not dovrei avere.

points.point: the conditional for unconfirmed news (si sarebbe dimesso)
points.explain: Journalists use the conditional to report claims they haven't confirmed: il sindaco si sarebbe dimesso.
points.trap: It doesn't mean 'would'; it signals 'reportedly'.

points.point: Lei imperatives (giri, vada, prenda) understood, not yet produced
points.explain: Strangers giving directions use Lei commands like giri (turn), vada (go), prenda (take).
points.trap: These look like 'wrong' endings (giri for an -are verb), so learners don't recognise them as commands.

points.point: chiamate! as a plural command chunk; ho perso as a chunk ahead of the past tense
points.explain: In an emergency, chiamate un'ambulanza! speaks to everyone around; ho perso... reports something lost.
points.trap: To one person you know it's chiama!, to a stranger chiami!; English imperatives don't change.

points.point: imperative for tu, noi, voi (gira, prendi, andiamo, girate); irregular va', fa', da', di', sta'
points.explain: The tu command of -are verbs ends in -a (gira), of -ere/-ire verbs in -i (prendi); noi and voi are like the present.
points.trap: -are verbs flip the vowel: the command is gira, not giri (giri is the Lei form).

points.point: negative tu = non + infinitive (non toccare) — trap: not 'non tocca'
points.explain: To tell a friend not to do something, use non + infinitive: non toccare, non preoccuparti.
points.trap: English 'don't touch' tempts non tocca or non tocchi.

points.point: pronouns attach: aspettami, dimmi, prendilo (consonant doubles after va', fa', di')
points.explain: With tu, noi and voi commands the pronoun joins the end: aspettami, prendilo; after va', fa', di', da', sta' the consonant doubles (dimmi, fammi).
points.trap: Writing them apart (aspetta mi) or forgetting the double consonant (dimi); gli never doubles (digli).

points.point: Lei imperatives (giri, prenda, attraversi) understood; produced at B1
points.explain: Strangers use Lei commands with you: giri a destra, prenda il 64, attraversi la piazza.
points.trap: These use the opposite vowel to the tu form (giri vs gira), which makes them easy to mishear.

points.point: Lei imperatives understood (prenda, beva, torni)
points.explain: Doctors and pharmacists give instructions with Lei commands: prenda una compressa, beva molta acqua.
points.trap: Prenda sounds like a statement to English ears; it's an instruction.

points.point: Lei imperatives in instructions (compili, firmi, torni) — understood
points.explain: Officials give instructions in the Lei imperative: compili il modulo, firmi qui, torni domani.
points.trap: They sound like statements; firmi qui is an instruction, not 'you sign here'.

points.point: the Lei imperative uses the present subjunctive forms (giri, prenda, venga, vada, faccia, dica, sia, abbia)
points.explain: Polite commands use the Lei present subjunctive: giri a destra, prenda questa, venga pure.
points.trap: -are verbs end in -i and -ere/-ire in -a, the reverse of the tu command.

points.point: pronouns go before it: mi dica, si accomodi, me lo dia
points.explain: With Lei commands, pronouns go in front: mi dica, si accomodi, me lo dia.
points.trap: Attaching them as with tu (dicami, accomodisi) is wrong in modern Italian.

points.point: negative: non + the same form (non si preoccupi)
points.explain: To say 'don't' politely, put non before the Lei form: non si preoccupi.
points.trap: Not non preoccuparsi (that's for writing/signs) or non ti preoccupare (tu).

points.point: imperatives with pronouns recycled (dammi retta, vacci)
points.explain: Tu imperatives attach pronouns with doubling after monosyllables: dammi retta, vacci presto.
points.trap: Vai ci or dai mi are wrong.

points.point: congiuntivo presente: regular forms and sia, abbia, faccia, vada, possa, voglia, dia, stia, venga
points.explain: The present subjunctive swaps the vowel of the ending (-are → -i, -ere/-ire → -a), and many common verbs use the io stem (faccia, vada, venga).
points.trap: The three singular forms are identical, so add a subject pronoun if it's unclear (che tu sia).

points.point: after penso che, credo che, spero che, non credo che, può darsi che, ho l'impressione che
points.explain: After verbs of opinion, hope and doubt + che, the next verb goes into the subjunctive: penso che sia chiuso.
points.trap: English never shows the subjunctive, so learners keep the indicative (penso che è).

points.point: indicative after so che, secondo me, è vero che
points.explain: Certainty takes the indicative: so che è chiuso, secondo me è chiuso, è vero che è chiuso.
points.trap: Learners overcorrect and put the subjunctive after so che.

points.point: in speech many say 'penso che è': recognise it, but use the subjunctive
points.explain: In relaxed speech many Italians use the indicative after penso che; you'll hear it, but the subjunctive is the standard.
points.trap: Don't copy the indicative in formal settings; it can sound careless.

points.point: impersonal expressions + che + subjunctive: è meglio che, è importante che, bisogna che
points.explain: È meglio che, è importante che, bisogna che + subjunctive give advice to a specific person; with no specific person use the infinitive (è meglio riposare).
points.trap: English 'it's better for you to' becomes è meglio che tu..., not è meglio per te di.

points.point: congiuntivo passato (abbia dormito, sia arrivato)
points.explain: The past subjunctive is abbia/sia + participle, for an earlier action after a subjunctive trigger: spero che tu abbia dormito bene.
points.trap: Same auxiliary and agreement rules as the passato prossimo.

points.point: emotion + che + subjunctive: sono contento che, mi dispiace che, ho paura che, che peccato che
points.explain: Feelings about what someone else does take che + subjunctive: sono contento che tu sia venuto.
points.trap: English 'I'm glad you came' has no 'that' and no subjunctive.

points.point: congiuntivo imperfetto forms (avessi, fossi, facessi, potessi, venissi)
points.explain: The imperfect subjunctive adds -ssi, -ssi, -sse, -ssimo, -ste, -ssero to the stem: avessi, potessi; essere is fossi.
points.trap: Io and tu forms are identical (se io avessi / se tu avessi).

points.point: vorrei che + congiuntivo imperfetto
points.explain: Vorrei che + imperfect subjunctive says what you'd like someone else to do: vorrei che tu venissi.
points.trap: English 'I'd like you to come' tempts vorrei che tu venga or vorrei te venire.

points.point: congiuntivo imperfetto after a past main verb (credevo che fosse)
points.explain: After a main verb in the past, a subjunctive clause uses the imperfect subjunctive: credevo che fosse facile.
points.trap: Keeping the present subjunctive after a past verb (credevo che sia) is a common error.

points.point: congiuntivo trapassato (pensavo che fossi già partito)
points.explain: Avessi/fossi + participle is for something that had already happened before a past opinion: pensavo che fossi già partito.
points.trap: English 'had left' has no subjunctive marking.

points.point: subjunctive in relative clauses with an open antecedent (una casa che abbia)
points.explain: When you describe something you're looking for, not something specific, the relative clause takes the subjunctive: cerco una casa che abbia un giardino.
points.trap: English shows no difference between 'a house that has' (real) and 'a house that has' (wanted).

points.point: sarebbe meglio che + congiuntivo imperfetto
points.explain: After a conditional main verb, use the imperfect subjunctive: sarebbe meglio che tutti usassimo meno la macchina.
points.trap: Sarebbe meglio che usiamo mixes moods.

points.point: non per questo + subjunctive; non è che + subjunctive
points.explain: Non è che and non per questo deny an assumed reason and take the subjunctive: non è che siano chiusi.
points.trap: English 'it's not that they're...' has no subjunctive.

points.point: non dico che + subjunctive
points.explain: Non dico che + subjunctive softens disagreement: non dico che tu abbia torto.
points.trap: Without the subjunctive (non dico che hai torto) it sounds blunt.

points.point: è ora che + subjunctive
points.explain: È ora che + subjunctive means 'it's time that': è ora che i giovani vengano pagati di più.
points.trap: English 'it's time they were' uses a past form; Italian uses the present subjunctive.

points.point: corre voce / si dice che + subjunctive
points.explain: Hearsay expressions take the subjunctive: si dice che chiudano il mercato.
points.trap: The indicative makes it sound like established fact.

points.point: the subjunctive in relative clauses that set a requirement (qualcuno che si occupi)
points.explain: A relative clause describing what's required takes the subjunctive: cerchiamo qualcuno che si occupi del giardino.
points.trap: The indicative implies you've already found the person.

points.point: the optative subjunctive (che siate felici, voglia il cielo che, magari fosse)
points.explain: A subjunctive on its own can express a wish: che siate felici!, magari fosse sempre così!
points.trap: English uses 'may' or 'if only'; there's no main verb in Italian.

points.point: indirect questions with the subjunctive
points.explain: In careful speech and writing, reported questions take the subjunctive: ci ha chiesto se avessimo mai visto Pirandello.
points.trap: The indicative is acceptable in speech, but the subjunctive is the C1 norm.

points.point: chiunque / qualunque / dovunque + subjunctive
points.explain: Chiunque (whoever), qualunque (whatever) and dovunque (wherever) take the subjunctive: chiunque abbia vissuto qui sa che...
points.trap: The indicative is a common slip.

points.point: se + present → present or future (real conditions)
points.explain: For real, likely conditions, use se + present (or future) and present or future in the result: se piove, restiamo a casa.
points.trap: If the 'if' clause is about the future, Italian may use the future too (se verrai, ci divertiremo), unlike English.

points.point: se + congiuntivo imperfetto, then the conditional — trap: never 'se avrei'
points.explain: For unlikely or imaginary conditions: se + imperfect subjunctive, then the conditional: se avessi tempo, viaggerei.
points.trap: English 'if I would' leads to se avrei, the classic error; 'if I were you' is se fossi in te.

points.point: se + congiuntivo trapassato → condizionale passato; mixed: past condition, present result
points.explain: For past conditions that didn't happen: se + trapassato subjunctive, then the past conditional; if the result is in the present, use the present conditional.
points.trap: Se l'avrei saputo is wrong; it's se l'avessi saputo.

points.point: the colloquial imperfetto in hypotheses (se lo sapevo, venivo) — recognise
points.explain: In casual speech both halves of a past hypothesis may be in the imperfect: se lo sapevo, non venivo.
points.trap: It looks like 'if I knew' (present), but it means 'if I had known'.

points.point: real conditions as promises or threats
points.explain: Se + present or future with a future result frames a firm promise or warning: se non risolvete il problema, faccio reclamo.
points.trap: Don't use the conditional for a real threat; it sounds hypothetical.

points.point: conditional + congiuntivo imperfetto in requests (Le sarei grato se potesse)
points.explain: Formal requests pair the conditional with se + imperfect subjunctive: Le sarei grato se potesse rispondermi.
points.trap: Se potrebbe is the error to avoid.

points.point: congiuntivo trapassato in counterfactuals
points.explain: Unreal past conditions use se + trapassato subjunctive: se non fossero emigrati, oggi non avrei parenti in Argentina.
points.trap: Se non sarebbero emigrati is the error.

points.point: come si dice? as a fixed impersonal si
points.explain: Come si dice...? means 'how do you say...?', using si for 'one/people'.
points.trap: Don't translate 'you' literally (come dici?) when you mean 'how does one say'.

points.point: si as a chunk: dove si comprano?
points.explain: Si + verb means 'one / people': dove si comprano i biglietti? = where do you buy tickets?
points.trap: The verb agrees with the plural thing (si comprano i biglietti), unlike English 'you buy'.

points.point: si può cambiare? as a chunk
points.explain: Si può + infinitive asks whether something is allowed or possible: si può cambiare?
points.trap: Not posso cambiare? if you mean the shop's rule in general.

points.point: mi hanno rubato: the impersonal 'they' where English uses a passive
points.explain: Italian often uses an unnamed 'they' instead of a passive: mi hanno rubato il portafoglio.
points.trap: English 'my wallet was stolen' tempts è stato rubato, which is correct but less natural in speech.

points.point: the passive with essere in the past (è stata costruita) as a chunk
points.explain: Essere + participle makes the passive: la chiesa è stata costruita nel Trecento.
points.trap: The participle agrees with the subject (chiesa → costruita).

points.point: si può / si possono
points.explain: Si può + infinitive asks if something is allowed; with a plural object, si possono: si possono fare foto?
points.trap: The verb agrees with the plural object, unlike English 'can you'.

points.point: impersonal si (si vive)
points.explain: Si + 3rd person singular states what people in general do: in campagna si vive meglio.
points.trap: Adjectives after si è are plural (quando si è stanchi).

points.point: the passive with essere (all tenses) and venire (simple tenses)
points.explain: Passives use essere + participle in any tense, or venire + participle in simple tenses to stress a process: le domande vengono esaminate.
points.trap: Venire can't be used in compound tenses (è venuto esaminato is wrong); the agent is introduced by da.

points.point: andare + past participle = must be done (va convalidato)
points.explain: Andare + participle means something must be done: il biglietto va convalidato.
points.trap: It isn't about 'going'; va convalidato = has to be validated.

points.point: the passive with modals (deve essere presentata)
points.explain: A modal + essere + participle makes a passive obligation or possibility: deve essere presentata entro giugno.
points.trap: The participle agrees with the subject (la domanda → presentata).

points.point: si passivante agrees with its noun (si accettano carte); impersonal si vs passive si
points.explain: With an object, si + verb agrees with it (si vendono case); without one, si + singular verb is impersonal (si mangia bene).
points.trap: Si vende case is the typical mistake.

points.point: the passive with venire for processes
points.explain: Venire + participle describes how something is regularly done: la ceramica viene cotta nel forno.
points.trap: Using essere can make it sound like a state rather than a process.

points.point: the impersonal 3rd plural (hanno rubato, l'hanno arrestato)
points.explain: An unnamed 'they' reports events where English uses a passive: l'hanno arrestato ieri.
points.trap: It doesn't refer to anyone specific; don't ask chi?

points.point: passive and impersonal recycled
points.explain: Formal letters favour passives and impersonals to sound neutral: si segnala che..., è stato effettuato il pagamento.
points.trap: Don't overload a short email with them.

points.point: andare + participle in procedures
points.explain: In procedures andare + participle states what must be done: la dichiarazione va presentata entro ottobre.
points.trap: It works only in simple tenses.

points.point: the passive and impersonal recycled
points.explain: Medical talk uses passives and impersonals: è stato ricoverato, si consiglia il riposo.
points.trap: Keep the agreement on the participle.

points.point: the passive with modals and with andare
points.explain: Rules use passives with modals or andare: i rifiuti vanno portati, le spiagge dovrebbero essere ripulite.
points.trap: Andare + participle can't combine with a modal (deve andare portato is wrong).

points.point: impersonal si in decisions (si è deciso)
points.explain: Si + essere reports collective decisions: si è deciso di rifare la facciata.
points.trap: Compound tenses with si always take essere.

points.point: si impersonale, passivante and riflessivo; ci si
points.explain: Si can be impersonal (si vive), passive (si vendono case) or reflexive (si lava); a reflexive verb made impersonal uses ci si (ci si abitua).
points.trap: Si si abitua is wrong; it's ci si abitua.

groups.name: Sequence of tenses and reported speech

points.point: the sequence of tenses: penso che venga / pensavo che venisse
points.explain: The tense of the subjunctive follows the main verb: present main → present subjunctive, past main → imperfect subjunctive.
points.trap: English doesn't shift; Italian does, and mismatches sound wrong.

points.point: indicative after past certainty (sapevo che era)
points.explain: After certainty in the past, keep the indicative: sapevo che era chiuso.
points.trap: Don't put the subjunctive after sapere just because the clause is in the past.

points.point: reporting with a past verb: present → imperfetto, passato prossimo → trapassato, future → condizionale passato (ha detto che sarebbe venuto — trap: not 'verrebbe')
points.explain: After a past reporting verb, tenses shift back; a future becomes the past conditional: ha detto che sarebbe venuto.
points.trap: English 'said he would come' tempts the present conditional (verrebbe), which is wrong.

points.point: reported questions with se and question words (indicative in speech, subjunctive in writing)
points.explain: Yes/no questions are reported with se, others with the question word: mi ha chiesto se mi trovavo bene.
points.trap: No question mark and no inversion; the subjunctive (se mi trovassi) is more formal.

points.point: no shift after a present verb (dice che...)
points.explain: After a present reporting verb (dice che), keep the original tenses: dice che non ce la fa.
points.trap: Don't backshift when the reporting verb is present.

points.point: reported speech recycled
points.explain: Passing on news uses reported speech with its shifts: mi hanno detto che l'avevano già arrestato.
points.trap: Keep the trapassato for things that had happened before the report.

points.point: the future in the past with the condizionale passato
points.explain: A future seen from the past uses the past conditional: ha dichiarato che non si sarebbe ricandidato.
points.trap: Not non si ricandiderebbe.

points.point: reported speech with all its shifts, at C1 accuracy
points.explain: Report statements, questions and orders with full tense, pronoun and time shifts.
points.trap: Forgetting pronoun shifts (mio → suo) is the usual slip at this level.

parts_of_speech.name: Verbals: infinitive, gerund, participles, causative fare

points.point: prima di + infinitive
points.explain: Prima di + infinitive means 'before doing': prima di trasferirmi.
points.trap: English uses '-ing' after 'before'; Italian uses the infinitive.

points.point: verb + a / di + infinitive: imparare a, provare a, cercare di
points.explain: Some verbs link to an infinitive with a (imparare a, provare a), others with di (cercare di, decidere di), and modals with nothing.
points.trap: Each verb's preposition must be learned; English 'try to' gives no clue.

points.point: dire di + infinitive as a chunk
points.explain: Dire a qualcuno di + infinitive reports advice or orders: il medico mi ha detto di riposare.
points.trap: English 'told me to' becomes mi ha detto di, not mi ha detto a or che riposare.

points.point: prima di + infinitive
points.explain: Prima di + infinitive says what you do before something else, with the same subject: prima di firmare.
points.trap: Not prima firmare or prima di firmando.

points.point: stare + gerund in the past (stavo cucinando); stare per + infinitive
points.explain: Stavo + gerund is an action in progress when something happened; stare per + infinitive means 'be about to'.
points.trap: The plain imperfect (cucinavo) is often enough; stare per isn't 'stay for'.

points.point: same subject → di + infinitive (spero di tornare)
points.explain: When both parts have the same subject, use di + infinitive instead of che + subjunctive: spero di venire.
points.trap: Spero che io venga is wrong.

points.point: prima di + infinitive (same subject) vs prima che + subjunctive
points.explain: Prima di + infinitive when the subject is the same, prima che + subjunctive when it changes.
points.trap: Prima che io parta is wrong; it's prima di partire.

points.point: same subject → di + infinitive (sono contento di vederti)
points.explain: If the feeling and the action share a subject, use di + infinitive: mi dispiace di non poter venire.
points.trap: Sono contento che io ti veda is wrong.

points.point: infinitives on signs and in instructions (spingere, non fumare)
points.explain: Signs, recipes and forms give instructions in the infinitive: spingere, non fumare, compilare in stampatello.
points.trap: English signs use the imperative or a noun ('No smoking'); Italian infinitives are commands.

points.point: commands → di + infinitive
points.explain: Reported orders and requests use di + infinitive: mi ha detto di non lasciare le bici.
points.trap: Not mi ha detto che non lascio or mi ha detto a non lasciare.

points.point: pur + gerund for concession (same subject in both parts)
points.explain: Pur + gerund means 'although / even while': pur vivendo qui da anni, ho ancora l'accento.
points.trap: Both parts must share the subject; otherwise use benché + subjunctive.

points.point: the gerund for means, cause and time, with pronouns attached (leggendolo); the past gerund (avendo letto)
points.explain: The gerund (-ando/-endo) expresses 'by/while/since doing'; pronouns attach to it, and avendo/essendo + participle marks an earlier action.
points.trap: The gerund must share the main subject, and it's not used after prepositions (prima di leggere, not prima di leggendo).

points.point: the past infinitive (dopo aver letto; mi sembra di averlo letto)
points.explain: Avere/essere + participle in the infinitive refers to an earlier action: dopo aver letto, mi sembra di averlo già visto.
points.trap: English 'after reading' tempts dopo leggere or dopo leggendo.

points.point: the absolute participle (finito il libro, ...)
points.explain: A past participle alone can open a sentence to mean 'once X was done': finito il libro, ne ho comprato un altro.
points.trap: The participle agrees with its own noun (finita la lezione).

points.point: fare + infinitive (far riparare); farsi fare (mi sono fatto tagliare i capelli); lasciare + infinitive
points.explain: Fare + infinitive means 'have something done' (faccio riparare la caldaia), farsi + fare 'have it done for yourself', lasciare + infinitive 'let'.
points.trap: English 'get my hair cut' tempts prendere or avere; it's farsi tagliare i capelli.

points.point: past infinitive after dopo and per (dopo aver parlato, per essere uscito)
points.explain: Dopo + past infinitive means 'after doing', per + past infinitive gives a past cause: rimproverato per essere uscito.
points.trap: English '-ing' tempts dopo parlando or per uscendo.

points.point: infinitive vs subjunctive (preferisco operarmi / preferisco che mi operi lui)
points.explain: Same subject → infinitive; different subject → che + subjunctive: preferisco operarmi vs preferisco che mi operi lui.
points.trap: Preferisco che io mi operi is wrong.

points.point: gerund and participle clauses (non avendo ricevuto)
points.explain: Gerund and participle clauses compress formal sentences: non avendo ricevuto risposta, ...
points.trap: The implied subject must match the main clause.

points.point: pur + gerund; senza + infinitive
points.explain: Pur + gerund concedes (pur essendo giovane), senza + infinitive means 'without doing' (sembrano italiani senza esserlo).
points.trap: English 'without being' tempts senza essendo.

points.point: molto as adverb (invariable) vs adjective (agrees)
points.explain: Molto before an adjective or after a verb never changes (molto bello, parla molto); before a noun it agrees (molte persone).
points.trap: Molta bella is wrong; buono is the adjective, bene the adverb.

points.point: time words: ieri, sabato scorso, due giorni fa; sequence: prima, poi, alla fine
points.explain: Fa after a time means 'ago' (due giorni fa), scorso means 'last' and agrees (la settimana scorsa).
points.trap: 'Ago' goes after the time, and 'last week' is la settimana scorsa, not l'ultima settimana.

points.point: frequency: di solito, spesso, ogni tanto, non... mai
points.explain: Frequency words usually go after the verb; 'never' is non + verb + mai.
points.trap: Italian needs the double negative: non vado mai, not vado mai.

points.point: appena and quando with the future
points.explain: Appena and quando take the future when the action is future: ti chiamo appena arrivo / arriverò.
points.trap: English uses the present after 'as soon as'; both are accepted in casual Italian, the future in careful speech.

points.point: time and place shifts: domani → il giorno dopo, qui → lì
points.explain: Reporting later shifts time and place words: domani → il giorno dopo, ieri → il giorno prima, qui → lì.
points.trap: Forgetting to shift makes the report sound like it's still today.

points.point: -mente adverbs and their position
points.explain: Adverbs in -mente are built on the feminine adjective (lentamente); they usually follow the verb, and in compound tenses often the participle.
points.trap: Adjectives in -le/-re drop the e (facilmente), and some adverbs like affatto must sit after non + verb.

points.point: di + city for origin (sono di Chicago); a + city, in + country (abito a Firenze, in Italia)
points.explain: Use essere di for where you're from, a with a city and in with a country or region.
points.trap: English uses 'from' and 'in' for everything; abito in Firenze and sono da Chicago are classic errors.

points.point: places with a, in, da as chunks: al bar, alla stazione, in piazza, in farmacia, dal medico
points.explain: Each kind of place goes with its own preposition, best learned as a chunk: in farmacia, al bar, dal medico (at the doctor's).
points.trap: English uses 'at/to' for everything; da + person (dal medico, da Marco) has no English equivalent.

points.point: articulated prepositions met as chunks (al, alla, nel) before the table is taught
points.explain: A, da, in, di and su merge with 'the': a + il = al, in + la = nella, da + il = dal.
points.trap: Learners say a il or in la; these always combine.

points.point: place words: vicino a, accanto a, davanti a, di fronte a, in fondo a, a destra, a sinistra
points.explain: Most place words need a after them before a noun: vicino alla stazione, davanti al bar.
points.trap: Forgetting the a (vicino la stazione) is the most common slip; di fronte a = opposite, not 'in front of' (davanti a).

points.point: alle + hour (all'una, a mezzogiorno); dalle ... alle ...
points.explain: 'At' a time is alle + hour (all'una, a mezzogiorno), and opening hours run dalle 9 alle 13.
points.trap: Don't say a le tre or in tre; dalle...alle replaces 'from...to'.

points.point: tra + time for 'in ten minutes' (trap: in dieci minuti means 'taking ten minutes')
points.explain: Tra (or fra) + time says when something will happen from now: torno tra dieci minuti.
points.trap: In dieci minuti means 'within/taking ten minutes', so English 'in ten minutes' is usually tra.

points.point: quantity + di: un chilo di, mezzo chilo di, un etto di, un litro di
points.explain: A quantity word is linked to the food with di: un chilo di pomodori, due etti di prosciutto.
points.trap: An etto is 100 grams; English speakers drop the di (un chilo pomodori).

points.point: rooms take in: in cucina, in bagno, in camera
points.explain: Rooms of the house use in with no article: in cucina, in bagno, in camera.
points.trap: Don't add the article (nella cucina) unless you mean a specific kitchen described further.

points.point: in + transport (in treno, in autobus) but a piedi
points.explain: Means of transport take in with no article (in treno, in macchina), but on foot is a piedi.
points.trap: English 'by/on' becomes in; in piedi means 'standing'.

points.point: per + destination (un biglietto per Firenze)
points.explain: A ticket or train 'to' a place uses per: il treno per Roma.
points.trap: Learners say a Firenze, which is fine for going but not for a ticket.

points.point: secondo me / per me + indicative
points.explain: Secondo me and per me ('in my opinion') are followed by an ordinary indicative verb.
points.trap: Learners who know penso che + subjunctive wrongly add the subjunctive here too.

points.point: in with plural countries takes the article: negli Stati Uniti
points.explain: Most countries take plain in (in Italia), but plural ones take the article: negli Stati Uniti.
points.trap: In Stati Uniti sounds wrong; so does in Italia with an article unless qualified.

points.point: per + finished time (ho lavorato per vent'anni) vs da + ongoing (lavoro qui da un anno)
points.explain: Per + time with the past is for a finished period; da + time with the present for something still going on.
points.trap: Ho lavorato qui da un anno mixes the two.

points.point: nominal style: in merito a, a seguito di
points.explain: Formal writing prefers noun phrases with compound prepositions: in merito a (regarding), a seguito di (following).
points.trap: Using them in speech sounds bureaucratic.

points.point: verbs + preposition (contare su, dare retta a, fidarsi di)
points.explain: Many verbs require a specific preposition: contare su, dare retta a, fidarsi di, dipendere da.
points.trap: English prepositions don't transfer (trust in = fidarsi di).

points.point: mentre + imperfetto; c'era / c'erano
points.explain: Mentre (while) introduces a background action in the imperfect; c'era/c'erano say 'there was/were' in a description.
points.trap: 'While I was waiting' is mentre aspettavo, not mentre sono aspettato.

points.point: connectives: siccome, visto che, perché, quindi, perciò, però, invece, così
points.explain: Siccome and visto che give the cause first, perché after; quindi and perciò give the result; però and invece contrast.
points.trap: Siccome goes at the start of the sentence; perché can't.

points.point: conjunctions with the subjunctive: purché, a meno che non, benché, prima che, perché (= so that)
points.explain: Purché (as long as), a meno che non (unless), benché (although), prima che (before) and perché meaning 'so that' take the subjunctive.
points.trap: Perché + indicative means 'because'; + subjunctive means 'so that'. A meno che needs a non that isn't negative.

points.point: anche se takes the indicative
points.explain: Anche se (even though/even if) takes the ordinary indicative: anche se fa freddo, esco.
points.trap: Learners who know benché + subjunctive put the subjunctive after anche se too.

points.point: come se + congiuntivo imperfetto; magari + congiuntivo imperfetto
points.explain: Come se (as if) and magari (if only) take the imperfect subjunctive: parla come se fosse il sindaco; magari avessi un balcone!
points.trap: English 'as if he were' sometimes uses 'is', but Italian always needs the subjunctive here.

points.point: nonostante + noun, or + subjunctive
points.explain: Nonostante + noun means 'despite'; nonostante + clause takes the subjunctive: nonostante piova.
points.trap: Nonostante + indicative (nonostante piove) is a common slip.

points.point: da quando + past, then present
points.explain: Da quando + past tells when something started, with the current state in the present: da quando ho cambiato operatore, non ho rete.
points.trap: English perfect 'I haven't had' becomes the present (non ho).

points.point: connectives: però, tuttavia, invece, anzi, infatti, comunque, inoltre, quindi, d'altra parte
points.explain: Connectives structure an argument: tuttavia (however), anzi (on the contrary/in fact), infatti (indeed), inoltre (moreover).
points.trap: Infatti confirms what was just said; it isn't 'in fact' as a correction (that's anzi or in realtà).

points.point: concessives: benché / sebbene + subjunctive vs anche se + indicative
points.explain: Benché and sebbene take the subjunctive, anche se the indicative.
points.trap: Mixing them (anche se sia) is very common.

points.point: benché / nonostante / sebbene / malgrado + subjunctive vs anche se + indicative
points.explain: All concessive conjunctions take the subjunctive except anche se.
points.trap: Benché è ben retribuito should be benché sia.

points.point: bureaucratic connectors: con la presente, a fronte di, ai sensi di, il suddetto, altresì
points.explain: Formal letters use set connectors: con la presente (hereby), ai sensi di (under), il suddetto (the aforesaid), altresì (also).
points.trap: They are for writing only; in speech they sound comic.

points.point: qualora + congiuntivo
points.explain: Qualora (should / in case) takes the subjunctive: qualora non fosse possibile, La prego di avvisarmi.
points.trap: Qualora + indicative is wrong; in speech se is enough.

points.point: correlatives: non solo... ma anche
points.explain: Non solo... ma anche links two points with emphasis: non solo non ha smentito, ma ha anche rilanciato.
points.trap: Keep both halves; ma anche can't be dropped as easily as English 'but also'.

points.point: result clauses (talmente... che, così... da)
points.explain: Talmente/così/tanto... che + indicative, or così... da + infinitive, express a result: era talmente bravo che...
points.trap: Da + infinitive needs the same subject.

points.point: formal connectors: bensì, eppure, pertanto, tuttavia, ossia, nonché
points.explain: Bensì (but rather, after a negative), eppure (and yet), pertanto (therefore), ossia (that is), nonché (as well as) give formal precision.
points.trap: Bensì only follows a negative (non X, bensì Y), and all of these sound bookish in casual talk.

points.point: ammesso che / posto che + subjunctive; the types of subordinate clause
points.explain: Ammesso che / posto che (assuming that) take the subjunctive; C1 control means choosing the right clause type (causal, concessive, conditional, final, consecutive).
points.trap: Ammesso che è vero is a common slip.

points.point: non goes right before the verb (non ho capito)
points.explain: To make a sentence negative, put non directly in front of the verb (or in front of the pronoun before the verb).
points.trap: There is no 'do not': don't look for a word for 'do', just put non in front.

points.point: questions by intonation, and question words chi, cosa, dove, come, quando, perché, quanto
points.explain: A yes/no question is a statement said with a rising voice; information questions start with a question word.
points.trap: There is no 'do' in questions (Parli inglese?, not 'Fai parlare...'), and the subject often goes after the verb (Dove abita Marco?).

points.point: dov'è / dove sono
points.explain: Dov'è asks where one thing is and dove sono where several things are.
points.trap: The apostrophe in dov'è is required in writing; the plural needs sono, not è.

points.point: sono le + hour, but è l'una, è mezzogiorno, è mezzanotte
points.explain: Telling the time uses sono le + number, except for one o'clock, noon and midnight, which take è.
points.trap: Che ore sono? is plural; English 'it is three' leads to è le tre.

points.point: qual è — no apostrophe
points.explain: Qual è...? asks 'what is...?' for names, addresses, numbers and passwords; it is written without an apostrophe.
points.trap: 'What is your password?' is qual è, not cos'è; and qual'è with an apostrophe is a spelling mistake.

points.point: double negatives: non... niente, non... nessuno, non... mai
points.explain: Italian requires non before the verb with niente, nessuno, mai and più: non ho visto nessuno.
points.trap: English forbids double negatives, so learners drop non.

points.point: di chi è? for whose
points.explain: Di chi è...? asks 'whose is...?', and the answer uses di or a possessive: è di Marco, è mio.
points.trap: There's no 's in Italian; 'Marco's' is di Marco.

points.point: question words in full: quale, quanto tempo, come mai, a che punto
points.explain: Quale asks which, quanto tempo how long, come mai why (surprised) and a che punto how far along.
points.trap: Come mai is softer than perché and doesn't invert the verb (come mai sei qui?).

points.point: question words in full: quale / quali, quanto, come mai, da quanto tempo, di che cosa
points.explain: Questions with a preposition put it first: di che cosa si occupa? da quanto tempo lavora qui?
points.trap: English dangling prepositions ('what do you deal with?') can't be copied.

points.point: exclamations: che + noun or adjective
points.explain: Che + noun or adjective makes an exclamation: che bello! che peccato! che fortuna!
points.trap: No article or verb is needed: not che una bella giornata.

points.point: più che X, Y; non è che + subjunctive
points.explain: Più che X, Y corrects a description (più che riservati, discreti); non è che + subjunctive denies an assumption.
points.trap: 'Rather than' isn't piuttosto di + adjective here.

points.point: pleonastic non (per poco non, finché non)
points.explain: Some expressions include a non that isn't negative: per poco non perdevo il treno (I nearly missed it), finché non arriva.
points.trap: Reading it as a negative reverses the meaning.

points.point: cleft sentences (è X che...; non è che... è che...)
points.explain: A cleft puts focus on one element: è l'accento che ti frega; non è che non voglia, è che sono stanco.
points.trap: English clefts are similar, but non è che takes the subjunctive.

parts_of_speech.name: Register, set phrases and discourse markers

points.point: greeting by time of day: buongiorno, buonasera, buonanotte only at bedtime; salve as a safe neutral hello
points.explain: Buongiorno until early afternoon, buonasera from mid-afternoon, buonanotte only when someone is going to bed, and salve when you're unsure how formal to be.
points.trap: 'Good night' as a goodbye in the evening is buonasera, not buonanotte.

points.point: courses as fixed phrases: come primo, come secondo, per dolce
points.explain: Ordering by course uses come primo..., come secondo..., per dolce... .
points.trap: Il secondo is the main course, not a 'second helping'.

points.point: the tu / Lei switch: darsi del tu, dare del Lei
points.explain: Dare del tu / del Lei means using tu or Lei with someone; possiamo darci del tu? proposes the switch.
points.trap: The older or higher-status person normally offers tu; switching on your own can feel rude.

points.point: phone formulas (pronto, chi parla?, la richiamo)
points.explain: Phone calls open with pronto, ask chi parla? and close with la richiamo (I'll call you back, Lei).
points.trap: Pronto is only for answering the phone; it's not 'hello' in the street.

points.point: spelling with city names (A come Ancona)
points.explain: Italians spell names using city names: B come Bologna, C come Como.
points.trap: English letter names (and j, k, w, x, y) confuse listeners; use the city alphabet.

points.point: clarifying: cioè, nel senso che, mi spiego
points.explain: Cioè, nel senso che and mi spiego meglio introduce a clearer version of what you meant.
points.trap: Overusing cioè as a filler sounds teenage; use it to clarify.

points.point: formal letter openings and closings (Gentile..., Egregio..., Cordiali saluti, Distinti saluti)
points.explain: Formal emails open with Gentile + title + surname and close with Cordiali saluti or Distinti saluti.
points.trap: 'Dear' is not Caro in formal writing, and there's no comma-plus-name sign-off like 'Best,'.

points.point: set reactions of outrage and indifference
points.explain: Fixed phrases like che faccia tosta!, è il colmo!, e allora? and e con ciò? react to news.
points.trap: Some indifference phrases (chi se ne frega) are rude; keep them for close friends.

points.point: the formal register in writing: Lei, often capitalised (Le, Suo)
points.explain: Formal emails use Lei throughout, often written with a capital (Le scrivo, la Sua risposta).
points.trap: Slipping into tu or voi mid-email jars; capitals are optional but consistent.

points.point: register: what's fine with friends but not with strangers
points.explain: Some words (casino, figo, un sacco) are fine with friends but out of place with officials or older strangers.
points.trap: Learners copy slang from friends into formal contexts.

points.point: discourse markers: ecco, diciamo, cioè, insomma, appunto, mah, vabbè, che ne so
points.explain: Discourse markers manage talk: diciamo softens, insomma sums up, appunto agrees, che ne so gives a vague example.
points.trap: Overusing them sounds like a tic; underusing them sounds stiff.

points.point: recognising dialect forms (Roman nun, pe', er, daje; Neapolitan features)
points.explain: Regional speech changes forms: Roman nun (non), pe' (per), er (il), daje (dai); Neapolitan drops final vowels.
points.trap: Don't copy dialect forms with strangers; recognise them.
